items.title: Ship attack reports near Hormuz reach record high as oil exports slow
items.summary: BBC Verify analysis of data from a UK maritime agency shows 12 vessels were struck in a week.
items.content:
The number of ships that have reported being attacked in and around the Strait of Hormuz has hit a record high, BBC Verify analysis of data from a UK maritime agency shows.

Twelve vessels were attacked between 5 and 11 October - the largest number of weekly strikes reported to the UK's Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency since the US-Israeli war with Iran began. The previous week saw 10 ships reporting attacks.

Six of the vessels were struck last Sunday, according to the UKMTO - a one-day high. So far this week, there have been four reported attacks.

As the number of strikes has risen, the recovery in oil shipments through the strait seen last month has slowed, industry data suggests.

BBC Verify collated incident reports published by the UKMTO on its website and created a timeline based on the first date cited in each report. This is approximate because some incidents use the date of the attack and some the date on which it was reported.

Experts say Tehran has been attacking ships in an effort to assert greater control over the waterway as the US military has increased the number of tankers it is shepherding through the south of the strait to evade Iranian strikes.

Iran is also carrying out more attacks on vessels further away from the Strait of Hormuz, according to experts.

The US military's Central Command, which oversees operations in the Middle East, posted on social media that despite the attacks "commercial traffic continues to flow through the Strait of Hormuz with co-ordinated protection from US forces and regional partners".

The aftermath of one of Sunday's six reported attacks was captured in verified footage showing the Nicaragua-flagged tanker Petro Dolphin on fire, as filmed by the crew on a smaller boat nearby.

The vessel was struck by a drone close to the Sohar Anchorage, Oman, more than 250km (150 miles) from the strait, according to the maritime intelligence firm Vanguard.

Eleven Indian seafarers were rescued but two are still missing, the Forward Seamen's Union of India said.

Attacks have continued this week with the container ship GFS Pride sinking after a strike by an unknown projectile in the strait on Tuesday. Twenty-one crew were safely evacuated.

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) published footage of what appeared to be the same ship sinking. It said the vessel was carrying "2,500 containers of contraband" and had taken an "unauthorised route".

Middle East oil exports have slowed as the number of ship strikes has risen.

About 12.6 million barrels per day went through the strait on 13 October, below the 15 million reported at the end of September, data from trade intelligence firm Kpler shows. This compares with a pre-war baseline of some 17 million barrels per day.

The recent increase in attacks comes as US Navy data indicates the number of vessels given assistance to navigate the Strait of Hormuz during the first 10 days of October was up 85% compared with the same period in August.

Most of the oil being shipped from Gulf Arab states recently has been carried using a "shuttle" system where a fleet of tankers load up and sail through the strait before transferring their cargo to larger tankers in the Gulf of Oman.

These shuttle ships use a route close to Oman's coastline. Iran says this is "unauthorised" and insist vessels take an alternative route closer to its own shore.

So-called assisted transits were a key factor in helping drive oil flows from the Middle East back towards pre-war levels in September. This does not include Iranian exports which have completely stalled as a result of the US blockade of Iranian ports and ships.

Martin Kelly, CEO of Orbital Risk Intelligence, said Iran has "evolved its strategy" in response to this loosening of its control over the strait and has been carrying out "near daily or multiple attacks every single day".

"The aim here is to stop the ships going through and to deter others," he added.

The IRGC's navy has said strikes would not be "limited to the Strait of Hormuz" and later announced a "new deployment formation" across the region, according to state media.

Martin Kelly told BBC Verify that Iran is widening its attacks and targeting ships near the coast of Gulf Arab states and in the Gulf of Oman.

A tanker was struck by multiple projectiles north of Qatar on Thursday 8 October, more than 500km (310 miles) from the strait, resulting in multiple reported casualties, according to Vanguard.

Another tanker was attacked close to the UAE town of Al-Jazirah al-Hamra on Friday 9 October, Vanguard said.

Verified footage shows crew members running across the deck and putting on lifejackets as a large cloud of black smoke rises over the ship.

items.title: They fled Russia, but the West sent them back
items.summary: Over the past year there has been a stark rise in anti-government activists deported to Russia from the EU and US where they were seeking refuge.
items.content:
Russian security services were waiting when the flight landed in Moscow in December. On board were Russians the US had deported, including activists denied political asylum.

"It was unbelievably frightening. My knees were shaking with fear," says Katya, one of the deportees. We have changed her name to protect her identity, as she remains in Russia.

Katya had left Russia and claimed asylum in the US two years earlier.

When Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, many countries publicly welcomed fleeing Russians. But more than four years later, attitudes have hardened. The numbers of anti-war Russians forcibly returned from Western countries is rising, and Katya's experience highlights the potential risks they face.

US authorities rejected her application for asylum, after she said she had provided evidence that she had taken part in protests and was a member of an opposition movement.

In Moscow, Katya says officers from the FSB security service handed all the male deportees military papers, requiring them to register with the local enlistment office, from where men are often sent to the war in Ukraine. Another passenger on the flight and an activist confirmed her account.

The officers interrogated her, and many others, for several hours.

"At one point, they found incriminating information on my phone," says Katya, "Their faces changed in a second. I was very afraid that they would simply bundle me off somewhere."

Katya was eventually released and allowed to stay with relatives. But she says police continue to call her and visit her at home.

"I feel as if I'm in a cage, like in a zoo," she says, "Whenever I see a police car, I feel terrified and start thinking, "What if they're coming for me?"

Katya showed the BBC documents and photographs confirming her story, which matches accounts from other deportees.

Removals from the US rose from 222 in 2023 to more than 1,200 in 2025, amid a wider increase in deportations under President Donald Trump's second term. Activists say Russian deportees included dissidents and Russian army deserters, some of whom were imprisoned or sent to war after returning to Russia.

One such case is Leonid Melekhin, an anti-war activist who sought asylum in the US after being arrested at protests in Russia. He had posted photographs of Russian President Vladimir Putin online with the message "Putin: murderer, fascist, usurper". After being deported back home last year, Melekhin was charged with "justifying terrorism" and sentenced to six years in prison.

"We have several examples of people who got eight years in prison when they crossed the [Russian] border," says Andrei Pivovarov, from Russia's exiled opposition Anti-War Committee.

And deportations are taking place from Europe too. His organisation has changed its advice to dissidents escaping Russia: the EU is no longer safe, it is better to seek refuge elsewhere.

Germany has sharply increased the number of Russian nationals it deports. Seven were sent back in 2023, rising to more than 110 in 2025, according to German government figures. More than 21,000 Russians sought asylum in Germany between 2022 and 2025, but the proportion of positive decisions fell from 29% in 2023 to just 6.8% in the first eleven months of 2025.

"Protection is only granted if there is an actual, well-founded fear of persecution," Germany's migration and asylum agency, BAMF, told the BBC.

Last year, Berlin suspended its humanitarian visa programme for Russians, and across the EU, the proportion of Russian applicants granted some form of asylum protection fell from 23% in 2024 to around 17% in the first nine months of 2025, according to EU data.

Russian opposition activists fleeing repression have become caught up in a wider crackdown on immigration, as governments across Europe and the US toughen rules amid political pressure over high numbers of irregular migrants and asylum applications, as well as over security concerns.

Western governments are "focused on limiting humanitarian programmes and asylum seekers", says lawyer Anastasia Burakova, founder of rights group Kovcheg (Ark), which helps anti-war Russians leave the country. The clampdown is "in response to public concerns and rising support for right-wing populist parties", she adds.

Following a negative asylum decision, Russian nationals are often given the chance to leave independently, but a rising number are being forcibly returned to Russia, usually escorted via third countries.

Several Russian activists in exile told the BBC that immigration officials had told them they faced "no danger" in Russia, and that officials often lacked an adequate understanding of the risks that activists face.

"I tried to explain that if they sent me back, I would be put in prison, or sent to war where I'd be killed," explains former soldier Artyom, who deserted from the Russian Army in 2022 after officers threatened to send him to Ukraine. "They just didn't believe me."

He says he provided US authorities with proof that a criminal investigation had been opened against him back in Russia for desertion. But he was put on a deportation flight back to Moscow via Egypt.

"I was preparing for death," says the former soldier, "I was thinking, 'how can I die without it being painful?'".

Back in Moscow, Artyom was held in a military detention facility but managed to escape. He is now in hiding abroad.

"Another country could investigate me better and give me asylum. Why didn't they give me that chance? Instead they deported me specifically to Russia," says the deserter. "It ruined my life."

The US Department of Homeland Security told the BBC: "All illegal aliens receive due process. If a judge finds an illegal alien has no right to be in this country, we are going to remove them."

The asylum clampdown comes as repression inside Russia has reached "an unprecedented level", according to Nobel Prize-winning Russian human rights group Memorial. Their list of political prisoners grew from 803 to 1,265 during 2025, a record increase.

The Russian Embassy in London did not respond to a request for comment.

Anti-war activist Mikhail says he and his wife Dasha are awaiting deportation from Finland "any day". Their names have been changed to protect their identity, as Mikhail fears for relatives back home.

Russian authorities blocked his social media accounts over anti-war posts, and police visited his mother and accused him of spreading "fake information".

Dasha is a Jehovah's Witness, an organisation banned as "extremist" in Russia. The couple provided Finnish authorities with evidence, seen by the BBC, including a video of Russian police telling his mother that more than 300 posts had violated Russian law. A single post can result in a long prison sentence.

The Finnish Immigration Service has rejected their asylum request five times, deciding there is "no reasonable basis to believe" the couple would face serious rights violations if returned.

"We're sitting here and someone could knock on our door at any moment, take us to the Russian border and simply hand us over to Russian officers," says Mikhail. "We fear for our lives!"

"We came to Finland for help, and they're refusing us," he adds. "My wife cries constantly."

Amnesty International, which is supporting the couple, says they could face a "real risk" of detention, prosecution, imprisonment and torture if returned.

The Finnish Immigration Service said all asylum decisions were based on international refugee law standards, and the share of Russian citizens receiving asylum was in line with EU averages.

For Mikhail and Dasha, the threat of deportation comes as more Russians may be considering leaving.

There are rumours that Vladimir Putin may announce a new wave of mobilisation to boost the ranks of his army in Ukraine, which the Kremlin denies. The last mobilisation in 2022 prompted hundreds of thousands of Russians to flee, many to ex-Soviet states such as Armenia and Georgia.

Anastasia Burakova's organisation says requests for help from Russians wanting to leave rose tenfold in August compared with May. For those now looking to escape, the question is whether the West will offer them refuge — or send them back.

items.title: Italy’s unusual primary showdown: the former rebel and the professor vying to take on Meloni
items.summary: Progressive voters will be asked to choose who should lead the opposition against the right. But deep divisions over military aid to Ukraine threaten to derail the alliance, while the battle for Italy’s presidency looms in the background
items.content:
Voters will decide who gets to challenge Giorgia Meloni at the ballot box in 2027. After a tortuous process in which every possible alternative was ruled out, including the basic principle that the leader of the largest party should head the coalition, Italy’s progressive alliance has finally resigned itself to letting voters decide through a primary election.

And given the relative weight of their parties, it will largely come down to an OK Corral-style showdown between Democratic Party (PD) leader Elly Schlein and Five Star Movement (M5S) president Giuseppe Conte.

The two leaders have radically different backgrounds and political histories. Their rivalry reflects a divide also playing out in Italy between a social-democratic left, rooted in Europe's traditional political families and firmly committed to supporting Ukraine, and a movement that has made opposition to arms deliveries to Kyiv and criticism of European rearmament plans a defining feature of its political identity.

But there is one enormous difference between what is happening in Italy and the rivalry between competing strands of the left in France and Germany, countries comparable in population, GDP, manufacturing strength and membership of the G7.

Unlike in other Western democracies, Italy's electoral law effectively forces parties to form competitive coalitions before an election, leaving no room for post-election parliamentary negotiations.

Both the previous electoral law, introduced by the centre-left in 2017, and the new one, approved at Giorgia Meloni's urging in early October amid fierce controversy and the prospect of numerous challenges before the Constitutional Court, make multiparty alliances a practical necessity.

Failing to form one means almost certain defeat, as the centre-left discovered in 2022. It went into that election split three ways: a small coalition comprising the PD and two smaller parties, the Greens and Left Alliance (AVS) and Emma Bonino's More Europe; the Five Star Movement running on its own; and the moderates of the Third Pole, also standing separately.

That three-way split allowed the centre-right to win most single-member constituencies, despite receiving fewer votes nationwide than its opponents combined.

It is a mistake Elly Schlein has promised "will never happen again". She has built her entire political strategy around the mantra of coalition unity as the only way to challenge the right-wing government.

But while agreement on the main economic and social issues appears within reach ahead of primaries that could take place in the first few months of 2027, observers are wondering how the foreign policy positions of the traditionally pro-EU, pro-Kyiv PD can possibly be reconciled with those of Giuseppe Conte.

Conte recently drew a political parallel between the Russian autocrat and the Ukrainian president, putting it this way:

"Putin, having committed a criminal act of aggression, bombs every day, just as Zelensky has also begun bombing Russian territory, and has been doing so for some time. I'm not defending Putin, but we cannot pretend that Zelensky's side is acting purely in self-defence, because they too have unfortunately been carrying out various attacks and bombings for some time now, including attacks that have affected civilians."

So the real question remains unanswered: can the new electoral rules, which require not only the formation of a multiparty coalition but also the designation of a leader accepted by all its members, overcome this profound foreign policy divide?

The paradox is that, judging the two leaders purely by their backgrounds, one might have expected Schlein, rather than Conte, to be the grassroots campaigner and activist more closely associated with pacifism and street protests.

Indeed, Schlein's entire political life before taking over the PD was defined by grassroots activism, often in opposition to the establishment.

Born in Switzerland to an Italian mother and an American father, Elena "Elly" Schlein was a rebel from childhood. Her parents sent her to piano lessons, but she secretly bought herself an electric guitar.

After finishing secondary school, she decided to move to Italy and enrolled in Bologna University's arts, music and performing arts programme, known as DAMS, to pursue her love of cinema. After a year, however, she switched to law, remaining in Bologna.

The city is famous in Italy not only for its university but also for its libertarian, open-minded and nonconformist youth culture.

Schlein graduated with a thesis on the rights of migrants and foreign nationals, then flew to the United States to volunteer for Barack Obama's 2008 presidential campaign.

Back in Italy, she attracted attention with the #OccupyPD protest against the leadership of the very party she would seek to lead.

Her relationship with the PD culminated in a dramatic break in 2015 over disagreements with the moderate policies of its then leader and prime minister, Matteo Renzi.

She eventually returned as the underdog and pulled off a surprise victory over Stefano Bonaccini in the party's leadership primaries.

Separated by 20 years in age, Schlein and Conte could hardly be more different in their professional backgrounds either, apart from the fact that both hold law degrees.

While the PD leader cut her political teeth as a grassroots activist, Conte was a reserved professor of private law, far removed from politics, until the Five Star Movement pulled him out of a hat like a rabbit.

And so, virtually unknown to Italians outside academic circles and his students at the University of Rome, Conte suddenly found himself prime minister in June 2018, heading an unlikely coalition between Beppe Grillo's Five Star Movement, founded as an anti-establishment force, and Matteo Salvini's League, a right-wing, Eurosceptic, anti-immigration party.

Even more surprising was Conte's dramatic about-turn. After leaving Salvini to his fate, he agreed, just 18 months later, to lead a government of the opposite political complexion, this time alongside the Democratic Party.

Given this long history of clashes and ruptures, including the troubled end of Mario Draghi's government — which collapsed after Conte's M5S withdrew its support — it is easy to see just how difficult it will be to build a credible coalition capable of replacing Giorgia Meloni, who has set a historic record for longevity in office at Palazzo Chigi.

But to grasp the full stakes, and why the contenders in the progressive primary showdown may have no choice but to reach an agreement, it is necessary to look beyond 2027.

In February 2029, the second term of Italy's president, Sergio Mattarella, will come to an end. Widely respected, Mattarella consistently tops opinion polls for his popularity among Italians across the political spectrum.

And it will be the majority in the next parliament that chooses his successor.

The Italian presidency is far from a ceremonial position. Under the Constitution, the occupant of the Quirinal Palace is the ultimate referee of Italian politics.

The prospect of Giorgia Meloni becoming the kingmaker in the election of the next president of the Republic — perhaps even claiming the country's most coveted office for herself — could prove the most powerful incentive for the two rivals in the progressive camp's OK Corral showdown to holster their guns and shake hands.

This article was reviewed by an external translation partner

items.title: Children aged 5, 8 and 11 killed in US school shooting before suspect shot by bystander
items.summary: A teacher was also killed in the attack at the Silver Rail Elementary School in the city of Bend, police say.
items.content:
A 16-year-old has shot dead three children and a teacher at a primary school in the US state of Oregon before he was killed by a bystander, police said.

The suspect, who has not been named, forced his way into Silver Rail Elementary School in the city of Bend on Thursday afternoon by shooting at locked doors, Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz confirmed.

The teenager was shot dead by a community member who "pursued him into the school and engaged him", Krantz said. Police arrived three minutes later.

The three children killed were aged five, eight and 11. A seven-year-old and a 54-year-old teacher were taken to a hospital in a critical condition. It is unclear if the attacker had any links to the school.

"We are stunned and heartbroken by this senseless tragedy," Steven Cook, the top administrative official of the local school district, said in a statement.

"No words can adequately express the grief our community is experiencing."

Police said the attacker was a local 16-year-old boy, but they did not release any further details on him or the identity of the victims.

Police were alerted to an active shooter at Silver Rail Elementary at 12:59 local time (19:59 GMT), Bend Police Department spokeswoman Sheila Miller told reporters.

The first call came from a person who said that an unknown suspect was shooting into their car with a long gun, police said. Photos released from the scene show a red truck with bullet holes.

Minutes later, the local county dispatch received 911 calls reporting that the attacker had entered the school.

Police said he shot at locks on the doors in order to force his way inside.

Local media reports suggested the school received new classroom doors in 2022 which can be locked with the flip of a switch.

A bystander saw the shooting begin to unfold, pursued the attacker into the school and shot him dead, police explained.

Three minutes later, officers first arrived at the scene. They confirmed that the attacker had been killed, and then searched the school.

Oregon Governor Tina Kotek praised the bystander who "heroically intervened" to stop further loss of life.

"Your actions carry a heavy emotional burden and I just want you to know that my thoughts are with you as well," she told a media briefing alongside other officials.

A local newspaper reporter told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that the school was in lockdown during the shooting and that students were able to communicate with parents outside with their Apple watches.

Michael Kohn, a reporter with Bulletin newspaper, said the incident had left the parents stunned.

"This is a neighbourhood school. Parents are stunned. It's just something you don't expect to happen in Bend, Oregon. It's a mountain town," he said.

Schools in Bend have been closed on Friday. Officials said the community needed time to heal.

Around 450 children attend Silver Rail Elementary School, which has more than 40 adult staff members, police said.

According to the K-12 School Shooting Database, there were 235 shooting incidents at American schools last year and at least 140 so far this year.

Gun control advocacy group Everytown for Gun Safety has ranked Oregon 12th in the list of US states on the strength of its gun laws.

But gun violence rate in the state is near the national average at 14.2 deaths per 100,000 residents, according to the group.

items.title: Roma capitale degli sfratti
items.summary: Anche in Italia studenti e inquilini manifestano per la crisi abitativa, ma le proteste sono frammentarie e poco raccontate. E le istituzioni non rispondono a una situazione che rischia di degenerare Leggi
items.content:
Deve fare la dialisi tre volte alla settimana ed è in attesa di un trapianto, ma il suo problema più grave è la casa. Maria Letizia Pietrangeli, 62 anni, è sotto sfratto nonostante la disabilità. Gli ufficiali giudiziari verranno ad assicurarsi che lasci la casa entro il 16 dicembre. Proprio a causa della malattia ha perso il lavoro e per questo non riesce più a pagare l’affitto: percepisce una pensione minima di 850 euro al mese che non le basta. “Sono in lista per una casa popolare da nove anni”, racconta.

Si è rivolta all’Unione degli inquilini, ma teme di non riuscire a trovare una soluzione prima di essere buttata fuori da casa e a quel punto non potrebbe neanche continuare a curarsi. “Ho lavorato per la provincia per più di dieci anni, ma la mia pensione è minima e non mi permette di comprare una casa né di pagare un affitto”, spiega. Ha una malattia autoimmune da quando era bambina e da quindici anni si deve sottoporre a dialisi.

Anche Manuela Messuri, 44 anni, un compagno e due figlie piccole, è nella stessa situazione dopo che il marito, un operaio edile, ha perso il lavoro. “Pagavamo 55o euro di affitto per una casa molto piccola ad Anagnina”, un quartiere della periferia sudorientale. “Stiamo tutti in una camera”, racconta. Da quando non riescono più a pagare rischiano lo sfratto. Messuri ha una bambina a cui è stata riconosciuta una disabilità grave, ma nonostante questo non ha avuto accesso all’edilizia popolare e si è rivolta allo sportello di Nonna Roma, un’associazione che aiuta le famiglie in difficoltà nella capitale. “Sono in graduatoria da cinque anni per una casa popolare”, racconta.

A Roma i casi come quello di Maria Letizia Pietrangeli e Manuela Messuri sono molti. Secondo i dati del ministero dell’interno pubblicati il 7 ottobre, in città ci sono quattro sfratti al giorno. Nel 2025 sono state in tutto 1.516 le famiglie della capitale e della provincia messe fuori di casa da un ufficiale giudiziario.

“I dati sugli sfratti relativi al 2025 evidenziano una diminuzione complessiva delle sentenze e delle esecuzioni, con una tendenza sostanzialmente omogenea in gran parte del territorio nazionale”, commenta Silvia Paoluzzi dell’Unione inquilini. Il 14 ottobre era a Bruxelles per incontrare insieme ad altri sindacati il commissario europeo con delega alla casa, Dan Jørgensen, che per la prima volta sta elaborando un piano europeo sulla questione.

“Le sentenze per morosità continuano a rappresentare la quota largamente prevalente del fenomeno. Rimane tuttavia il dato drammatico degli sfratti eseguiti con l’intervento della forza pubblica, che nella quasi totalità dei casi non sono accompagnati da alcuna soluzione abitativa alternativa per le famiglie coinvolte. Ci sono nuclei familiari costretti a dividersi per ricevere accoglienza in emergenza e i posti non sono sufficienti”, afferma Paoluzzi, secondo cui le persone che si rivolgono allo sportello dell’Unione inquilini perché non riescono a pagare l’affitto sono in aumento. Negli ultimi sei anni, i canoni di locazione a Roma sono saliti del 29,9 per cento , mentre i salari in Italia rimangono tra i più bassi d’Europa.

“Le persone arrivano a spendere il 50 o 60 per cento dello stipendio per la casa. Anche i nuclei familiari in cui ci sono due persone che lavorano non ce la fanno a pagare l’affitto”, spiega. Ma i sindacati degli inquilini non hanno molta forza contrattuale.

In Italia ci sono due canali per gli affitti: il canale del canone concordato e quello del canone libero introdotto dalla legge 431 del 1998 . “Questo doppio binario ci toglie forza negoziale”, afferma Paoluzzi, sottolineando che si dovrebbe ridefinire il significato di social housing . In Italia infatti i progetti di edilizia sociale sono affidati spesso ai privati, che finiscono per sfruttare anche questo settore per la speculazione. “Dobbiamo intenderci su cosa significa social housing. Per noi significa nuovi progetti di edilizia pubblica”, conclude la sindacalista.

In via Principe Eugenio 106, all’Esquilino, un quartiere centrale di Roma, c’è un appartamento di proprietà dell’Ater, l’azienda regionale per la gestione dell’edilizia residenziale pubblica, che potrebbe tornare nella disponibilità di una famiglia senza casa. Invece è in vendita. Il 13 ottobre Alberto Campailla dell’associazione Nonna Roma ha preso un appuntamento per visitarlo con un agente immobiliare: la base d’asta è di circa 600mila euro per 140 metri quadrati a due passi da piazza Vittorio.

“Al momento ci sono in graduatoria 16mila nuclei familiari che aspettano una casa popolare”, spiega Campailla poche ore dopo l’inizio della protesta, mentre gli attivisti sono ancora nella casa completamente da ristrutturare. “L’attesa per avere un alloggio può durare anche dieci o quindici anni”. Ogni anno a Roma si assegnano poche centinaia di abitazioni: “Una goccia nell’oceano”. Eppure, dal 16 al 20 ottobre, sul sito del notariato sono previste le aste per la vendita di trenta immobili dell’Ater. Secondo Nonna Roma, è ancora in corso un piano di vendita delle case di edilizia popolare, nonostante l’alta richiesta di case e l’insufficienza dei beni a disposizione.

Il paradosso, sottolinea Campailla, è diventato ancora più evidente dopo lo sgombero di Spin Time , l’occupazione abitativa che per tredici anni ha ospitato centinaia di persone. “A cento metri da qua c’è stato lo sgombero di Spin Time, dove sono state messe per strada quattrocento persone. Il comune sta cercando in tutti i modi di trovare una casa popolare per queste famiglie e ci vorrà tempo. Proprio nello stesso momento l’Ater, invece, le case le vende”.

Campailla racconta di aver parlato con un responsabile dell’azienda regionale durante la protesta. Secondo quanto gli è stato detto, nella maggior parte dei casi a interessarsi agli immobili sono delle società private, spesso straniere. Il timore è che queste abitazioni, anziché tornare a svolgere una funzione sociale, diventino strumenti di rendita o siano destinate agli affitti brevi turistici.

Intanto, a Roma gli sfratti continuano a colpire famiglie che non riescono più a sostenere il costo della loro abitazione. I numeri oscillano da un anno all’altro, ma il problema si intreccia con l’aumento degli affitti, i salari bassi e la crescita delle locazioni turistiche.

Non sono solo le persone in condizioni di povertà estrema a rischiare di perdere casa. “Prima ci occupavamo di chi viveva nelle case popolari o di chi, come dice la Caritas, era un equilibrista: un mese riusciva a pagare l’affitto, un mese rinunciava alle cure, un mese riusciva a fare la spesa”. Oggi, osserva Campailla, la difficoltà riguarda anche persone con stipendi ordinari, giovani coppie e lavoratori che non riescono a trovare un’abitazione compatibile con il loro reddito. Neppure un contratto a tempo indeterminato basta più.

La conseguenza è una progressiva espulsione degli abitanti dalla città. Se in passato le famiglie si spostavano dal centro verso le periferie, oggi sono costrette a cercare casa fuori Roma, a Guidonia, Tivoli, Ciampino o ai Castelli. “È un fenomeno di sostituzione sociale”, dice Campailla: non solo cambiano i quartieri, ma cambia la popolazione che può permettersi di abitarli.

Per l’attivista, una parte della risposta dovrebbe arrivare prima che lo sfratto diventi esecutivo. In Italia manca da anni un fondo nazionale adeguato per la morosità incolpevole, che consentirebbe ai comuni di aiutare chi non riesce a pagare l’affitto per una difficoltà economica sopraggiunta. “Sarebbe meglio aiutare le persone a conservare la casa”, insiste Campailla. “Il costo sociale di trovare un alloggio a una famiglia quando è già stata sfrattata è decisamente maggiore”.

Il 12 ottobre gli studenti dell’università Sapienza di Roma hanno piantato delle tende sotto la statua della Minerva, nel cuore della città universitaria. Nel frattempo l’Unione degli universitari (Udu) e altre sigle studentesche si accampavano di fronte al parlamento, nel centro di Roma, e incontravano alcuni rappresentanti delle istituzioni.

“Rivendichiamo il diritto alla casa, il diritto a un abitare che sia per noi dignitoso. Rifiutiamo la speculazione dei privati sugli studentati, che hanno prezzi inaccessibili “, afferma Marco Marino, studente e rappresentante di Piamo casa, coordinamento studentesco per il diritto all’abitare. Marino spiega che gli studenti hanno aperto uno sportello per capire quali sono i principali problemi abitativi di chi frequenta l’università e indirizzare le persone verso sindacati e istituzioni. “Si tratta anche di uscire da una condizione di isolamento e solitudine di fronte ai problemi materiali della maggior parte delle persone che frequentano l’università”, dice.

Da questa esigenza è partita la proposta del Forum sociale dell’abitare, una rete nata due anni fa che riunisce più di quattrocento organizzazioni tra movimenti, sindacati, associazioni e realtà del terzo settore. Hassan Bassi, tra i promotori dell’organizzazione, racconta che il Forum sta elaborando una proposta di legge nazionale e ha deciso di aprirla alla discussione nei territori a partire dal 14 ottobre. Una piattaforma online permetterà alle organizzazioni locali di commentare e integrare una prima bozza costruita intorno a dieci punti.

items.title: Come Israele scredita i giornalisti
items.summary: Che si tratti dei reporter uccisi nella Striscia di Gaza o dei registi di Naza, i leader politici e militari israeliani ricorrono a ogni mezzo per infangare chi non si allinea alla loro narrazione Leggi
items.content:
All’inizio di ottobre l’esercito israeliano ha pubblicato sul suo sito ufficiale in lingua inglese una lista di 170 giornalisti e operatori dell’informazione palestinesi uccisi durante la guerra nella Striscia di Gaza e considerati come “terroristi”. The press files , questo il nome della pubblicazione, si presenta come “un’indagine approfondita basata su un’ampia gamma di fonti d’intelligence, tra cui informazioni open source, documenti raccolti sul campo, interrogatori di agenti militari da parte dei servizi segreti israeliani e altro”. L’obiettivo è dimostrare che queste persone si dichiaravano giornalisti, ma ricoprivano invece ruoli “all’interno delle ali militari di organizzazioni terroristiche”.

Ogni nome, accompagnato da una fotografia, è seguito da numeri identificativi, dall’organo di stampa per cui la persona “a quanto pare lavorava come giornalista”, dall’“organizzazione terroristica” di cui faceva parte (Hamas o la Jihad islamica palestinese) e dalla posizione ricoperta al suo interno. In realtà, come dimostra un’analisi del giornalista ed esperto di Gaza Muhammad Shehada su +972 Magazine, le prove usate per accusare i giornalisti comprendono pagine vuote, documenti modificati e frammenti non verificabili.

Nei 49 casi più eclatanti le prove consistono in necrologi attribuiti direttamente a Hamas o alla Jihad islamica, che rivendicano le persone morte come loro affiliati. Ma anche questo “è lungi dall’essere conclusivo”, commenta Shehada. Di questi 49, infatti, 19 non sono mai stati inseriti nella lista dei giornalisti uccisi a Gaza compilata dal Committee to protect journalists (Cpj), di cui fanno parte 191 persone. Altri 21 sono stati rimossi dopo che è stato stabilito che non erano operatori dell’informazione o che avevano svolto un ruolo attivo nei combattimenti. Solo 78 nomi sui 170 nella lista dell’esercito israeliano compaiono anche nell’elenco del Cpj e nella grande maggioranza non sono accompagnati da foto incriminanti né da altre prove a sostegno delle accuse.

Le 59 schede relegate alla fine della lista sono prive di qualunque tipo di prova o documentazione e sono integrate semplicemente da un asterisco seguito dalla dichiarazione: “sulla base di diverse fonti di intelligence”. È il caso di Anas al Sharif, noto giornalista di Al Jazeera di 28 anni, ucciso il 10 agosto 2025 in un attacco aereo israeliano mirato contro una tenda di giornalisti all’esterno dell’ospedale Al Shifa; del suo collega Ahmed al Louh, cameraman di 39 anni ucciso nel campo profughi di Nuseirat; o di Hassan Sammour, della radio Sawt al Aqsa, morto insieme a undici componenti della sua famiglia quando una bomba israeliana ha centrato la sua casa a Khan Yunis.

L’esercito israeliano considera terroristi anche i giornalisti che sono entrati in Israele il 7 ottobre 2023, durante gli attacchi condotti da Hamas, senza considerare il fatto che molti di loro si sono precipitati nei dintorni della barriera che separa i due territori per documentare quello che stava succedendo. La scheda di Mohammed Abd al Aziz al Najjar, per esempio, contiene solo una foto di lui con le dita alzate in segno di vittoria e quello che sembra un veicolo in fiamme sullo sfondo. Quanto basta per etichettarlo come “agente militare” di Hamas.

In 19 casi le prove dell’esercito israeliano consistono in foto degli individui in posa con armi o con indosso uniformi militari, oppure in immagini riprese da video pubblicati dai gruppi estremisti palestinesi. “Inutile dire che essere ritratti in divisa militare o in posa con delle armi non significa automaticamente che una persona sia un militante”, nota Shehada. Che ricorda le foto pubblicate di Lizzy Savetsky, in cui l’influencer filoisraeliana è vestita con la divisa militare, ha un fucile in mano ed è circondata dai soldati israeliani. Inoltre dei 19 palestinesi solo quattro sono inclusi nella lista del Cpj, in seguito a indagini approfondite che hanno qualificato come “infondate” le accuse israeliane.

Oltre a essere privo di credibilità, questo tentativo israeliano di diffamare l’intera categoria dei giornalisti che continuano a raccontare al mondo quello che succede dentro la Striscia di Gaza va anche contro ogni logica, conclude Shehada. Perché mai un militante pericoloso e ricercato dovrebbe mostrarsi in pubblico, rivelare la sua posizione pubblicando aggiornamenti sui social media e trasmettere in diretta davanti a una telecamera con il rischio di essere colpito da un momento all’altro? E comunque, se proprio è convinto che tutti i giornalisti di Gaza sono legati a Hamas, Israele ha una soluzione facile per risolvere il problema: far entrare i reporter stranieri nella Striscia.

I leader israeliani, però, preferiscono di gran lunga infangare il lavoro di chi si oppone alla loro narrazione dei fatti e denuncia le atrocità commesse a Gaza. E per farlo non esitano a ricorrere a mezzi oscuri e scorretti, quasi al limite del ridicolo. È quello che sta succedendo con Naza: the real story , un film online promosso dal governo israeliano che è una specie di imitazione all’inverso di Naza , il documentario che dopo tre anni di genocidio raccontato dai giornalisti palestinesi finalmente sta facendo aprire gli occhi del mondo sui crimini dell’esercito israeliano a Gaza.

Proprio come il vero Naza , girato dai registi israeliani Yuval Abraham e Rachel Szor, anche il finto documentario si basa su interviste anonime fatte sui tetti di Tel Aviv. Ma invece di raccontare come il sistema di intelligenza artificiale viene usato dai militari israeliani per uccidere i civili a Gaza, le fonti si lanciano nella difesa dell’“esercito più morale del mondo”. Riproducendo anche lo stesso stile visivo, l’obiettivo è “rivelare nel dettaglio il sistema dietro l’uccisione di massa calcolata da parte di Israele dei terroristi a Gaza”, come si legge nella sinossi ufficiale, a sua volta una distorsione del senso dell’originale. Il progetto è ospitato sul dominio nazadocumentary.com , registrato il 16 settembre, sei giorni dopo la proiezione di Naza alla Mostra del cinema di Venezia, dove ha vinto il premio speciale della giuria.

I registi di Naza. The real story sono Ariel Averbuch, avvocato e riservista dell’esercito israeliano, e Roi Danino, candidato alle prossime elezioni con il partito di destra Israel first. L’8 ottobre il governo israeliano ha annunciato che i due registi saranno premiati con uno speciale documento chiamato “certificato di riconoscimento” per il loro “contributo alla diplomazia pubblica israeliana”. Abraham e Szor invece continuano a essere attaccati e demonizzati sui mezzi d’informazione e sulla scena politica israeliana.

L’11 ottobre il primo ministro israeliano Benjamin Netanyahu ha chiesto l’apertura di un’inchiesta contro gli esponenti delle forze di sicurezza che hanno testimoniato anonimamente in Naza, in modo da poterli perseguire penalmente per avere “danneggiato gli interessi diplomatici e di sicurezza di Israele”. Il Guardian, che ha prodotto il documentario, ricorda che “la protezione delle fonti giornalistiche costituisce un pilastro fondamentale della libertà di stampa secondo gli standard internazionali in materia di diritti umani e gli ordini di divulgazione sono ammessi solo a condizioni rigorose”. Secondo un portavoce del giornale britannico, tutte queste mosse sono un tentativo per “distogliere l’attenzione dalle questioni urgenti sollevate dal film riguardo alle uccisioni di massa di civili palestinesi a Gaza”.

items.title: Tesla svela la nuova Roadster con propulsori SpaceX. Uno show per Musk: l’auto vola
items.summary: Sviluppata con l’azienda aerospaziale, la versione più potente può decollare per brevi tratti e rimanere sospesa. Velocità massima 370km/h, produzione prevista nel 2028
items.content:
Se il tempo non è proprio volato, a volare ci pensa l’auto. A quasi nove anni di distanza dal primo modello, uscito nel 2008 e dismesso nel 2012, Tesla ha svelato la nuova generazione della della sua Roadster , una sportiva da strada a due posti capace di prestazioni impressionanti come lo 0-100 in meno di un secondo e 370km/h di velocità massima. Ma per l’azienda di Elon Musk non è stato un lancio qualsiasi, e “lancio” in questo caso sembra proprio la parola corretta: la Roadster 2.0 è dotata, oltre che delle più avanzate tecnologie del marchio, anche di speciali caratteristiche sviluppate in collaborazione con SpaceX , l’azienda aerospaziale di Musk. Ovvero, razzi ad aria che possono far decollare l’auto per brevi tratti e farla atterrare come un modulo spaziale, e un sistema di aspirazione che permette alla macchina di rimanere incollata alla strada anche capovolta. Questo almeno è ciò che si è visto durante la presentazione che si è svolta in un sito di prova di SpaceX in Texas. Una Batmobile fuori da Gotham City, una sorta di veicolo da fantascienza alla Blade Runner, ma che Tesla dice verrà prodotto in serie dal 2028.

Elon Musk ha dimostrato le caratteristiche della vettura, facendole percorrere una rampa a testa in giù grazie a un sistema di aspirazione, compiere una rotazione in aria, per poi atterrare utilizzando i propulsori integrati. In un altro stunt, la Roadster ha sorvolato un blocco composto da altri veicoli tesla, compreso un truck Semi, roteando in aria. “Le auto volanti sono una realtà”, ha detto Musk dopo la dimostrazione. Spettacolare sicuramente, anche dal punto di vista del marketing: non è stato immediatamente specificato se queste funzionalità potranno essere utilizzate legalmente sulle strade una volta che l’auto sarà in circolazione. Certo un regolamento specifico ancora non c’è e finora le auto volanti si sono viste solo nei film. E del resto i modelli di ispirazione per questa auto, dichiara Tesla, non sono altre automobili ma due aerei, l’ SR-71 e l’F-35 anche se il design rimanda inevitabilmente alle supercar e ai tratti decisi del Cybertruck. Ma come sarò omologata, e basterà la patente per guidarla o servirà un brevetto di volo? Viste le caratteristiche e le peculiarità tutte da normare, ci si chiede se questa Roadster volante arriverà mai davvero sul mercato o è destinata a rimanere un prototipo come innumerevoli altri veicoli presentati e mai apparsi nei listini nella lunga storia dell’automobile. In realtà l’auto è già ordinabile : la pagina delle prenotazioni sito Tesla mostra una versione Performance , per la quale è richiesto un deposito di 5000 euro e 45mila da versare entro dieci giorni, e una versione Thrust , dotata di “propulsori per l'accelerazione”, che richiede un deposito di 5000 e poi 245000 euro. Una terza variante, denominata Rocket , che Tesla dichiara disponibile esclusivamente su invito, viene descritta come un modello monoposto dotato di un “sistema di volo completo”.

Turns out the future does have flying cars https://t.co/6fexPp6SXI

Del resto Musk non ha fornito indicazioni sui prezzi previsti, anche se quasi dieci anni fa Tesla aveva annunciato un prezzo base di 200.000 dollari, già quindi superato dalla cauzione per la variante Thrust. Ma se dovesse arrivare ul mercato, l’analista di Morningstar Seth Goldstein prevede che Tesla venderà circa 2000 Roadster all'anno, un piccolo numero da boutique rispetto agli 1,6 milioni di veicoli venduti complessivamente dall'azienda lo scorso anno con Model Y e Model 3, che rimangono il core business del brand. La presentazione della Roadster di seconda generazione arriva peraltro in un momento in cui Tesla sta concentrando la propria attenzione anche verso le tecnologie di guida autonoma basate sull'intelligenza artificiale e sulla robotica, con Optimus, i Robotaxi e i Cybercab, e in cui l’azienda sta decisamente ridefinendo il suo perimetro.

items.title: Comparing Chromium Development at Google and Igalia
items.summary: Article URL: https://lwn.net/Articles/1094721/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50112887 Points: 43 # Comments: 14
items.content:
Sharon Yang is a Chromium developer who worked at Google on the browser and now works on it at Igalia. On the final day of FOSSY 2026, she gave a presentation on her experiences with both of those companies, comparing and contrasting the ways each one operates and how that affects work on the code base. She enjoyed working at Google and feels the same about Igalia, so the talk was not aimed at complaints—instead it was meant to give a feel for two companies that are rather different.

The talk was entitled "From Corporate to Co-op" highlighting one of the main differences between the enormous company, Google, and the employee-owned cooperative at Igalia. She is from Vancouver and went to the University of British Columbia, where FOSSY was held. While she was a student, she did an internship at Google, working on the Chrome browser, which is the Google product based on Chromium. In her slides , she showed a photo of herself—complete with propeller hat—in front of a Google sign.

When she was a student, her life was measured in semesters, but some of the people she worked with at Google had been working on Chrome for four years, which was amazing to her at the time. She ended up working at Google full-time for six years, all of it on Chrome. Most of her work was on the content layer of the browser, which is part of the open-source Chromium browser. So she works in the same repository ( GitHub mirror ), and with many of the same people, at Igalia as she did at Google. She briefly reflected on her time at Google: " I had a good time working on Chrome, the people were nice, I enjoyed it, it was cool, there was lunch, it was good stuff ", she said to laughter.

Eventually, she thought it might be time to move on, and perhaps out of the Seattle area where she was living, so she started looking around at the end of 2024. She had seen Igalia email addresses in the code base and met some of the people from the company at the BlinkOn conferences . Igalia is an open-source consulting company that is hired to work on various things, including Chromium; it is the largest contributor to Chromium that is not a browser maker, in fact. She joined Igalia and moved back to Canada a little less than a year before the talk in August.

She contrasted the two companies, starting with the number of employees: Google has around 180,000, while Igalia has around 180. In terms of revenue, last year Google had more than $400 billion, " Igalia, much smaller, we'll just say under a billion dollars ", which was greeted with laughter. Google is owned by institutional investors, while Igalia is owned by employees, which the audience applauded. Google has a wide range of compensation, from the CEO's $600 million salary package to her pay (somewhere in the range of $100,000-$300,000) when she worked there; at Igalia, all employees are paid the same, top to bottom and across the globe.

While they are " massively different entities ", both companies have teams working on things in common; she works on Chromium, but there are also teams from each working on accessibility and on web standards.

Chrome and Chromium are " kind of the same, they're kind of not ". Chrome is a Google product, with Google branding and colors, while Chromium is an open-source project that anyone can use to build a browser. Chromium is missing proprietary pieces like digital rights management (DRM), " AI integration ", and certain codecs; " and it's blue ". There are various other browsers based on Chromium, including Microsoft Edge and Brave , as well.

Most of the Google Chrome team members do most or all of their work in the Chromium repository. Obviously, the proprietary pieces are handled elsewhere, but she and other Google Chrome developers rarely have to interact with that code. Near the end of her time at Google, she had to get help to do a simple task that required access to the " totally different universe " where the proprietary parts live.

She then compared the experience of working for the two companies. The first week is pretty much the same at any new job, she said. The initial steps are getting to know your coworkers, reading internal documentation, learning how to communicate internally, and so on. Igalia has a whole set of open-source tools that it uses, which is nice.

There are some differences, as well. For example, there is a system for doing faster builds of Chromium, " otherwise you'll just spend all your time building Chromium ". That system is immediately available to Google employees, but external users have to request access to it. A bigger area of friction is access to bug reports, which are meant to be open to everyone unless they are security bugs. Due to a bug-tracker migration a few years ago, though, there are bugs that should be visible to outsiders, but are only visible to Google employees. " It is not a malicious thing ", and it is easy enough to get the access fixed, but it is something extra she has to do once a week or so.

There is other information that could be more readily available to the public, but is not because it is stored in Google Docs without being shared. Ensuring that the public has access " is a best-effort thing and people forget ", which is unfortunate. In addition, all of the tools for tasks like bug tracking are maintained by Google and, essentially, for Google, so outsiders have no way to provide feedback or request features and changes. They are " relatively minor points of friction " but they are enough to feel that " I am now separate from this ".

After a month in her new job, she started to see even more similarities with her previous one. The team members are all still available via the same communication channels (e.g. Slack), and she is likewise available to them. Some of the work that Igalia does comes directly or indirectly from Google; she is working a Chromium project that comes through the Linux Foundation, which Google is a member of. " I'm working on the same repository, I'm using the same tools, I'm getting money from Google, what's changed here? "

The answer it seems is " kind of everything and kind of nothing ". The types of projects are different at Igalia, though. At Google, she worked on the projects that were important to the people in her management chain; those are often new features or " a flashy metric that they want to improve ". They are often aimed at getting promotions for the engineers and those in the reporting chain.

The projects handed to Igalia to work on come directly from the technical staff, so they tend to be " code-health or tech-debt kind of projects ". For example, Igalia worked on componentizing the Chromium code base and its current project is " improving web-platform-test interoperability between browsers ". It is important work that is good to do, but " it is just so hard to imagine anyone at Google doing it for their day job "; it is " not the kind of work that gets prioritized or rewarded ". Many of the people that she worked with on Chromium at Google would love to be able to do that work. " These are people who care about the code base, they want it to be good, but there's just no room in their day job to do that, which is too bad. "

She was initially attracted to the Chrome team because all of the people on it seemed to be welcoming. That remained true throughout her tenure at Google and has continued into her work at Igalia. " People who work on Chromium have just generally been friendly and inclusive in all domains, which is good, and is not to be taken for granted. " She has been able to maintain relationships with her former coworkers, review their patches, leave comments on work that they have in common, and so on. " It's a nicer experience than sending a code review to some stranger. "

She put up a slide of an organization chart from a typical company, with her picture in a leaf node as the only filled-in box. In a chart like that, the engineer is at the bottom of the hierarchy; they have a manager, who has a more senior manager, and so on. An engineer is concerned with technical decisions, such as which language to use or how to test the code being written, while at the top, they are deciding things like company direction and vision. The people in the middle are doing some technical work, but it is often not entirely clear what it is that they do; " who knows? ", she said to laughter. " The people at the top are paid a lot more than the people at the bottom. "

At Igalia, things are quite different. The " org chart is intentionally flat " and there are no managers. There are various teams, such as the Chromium team that she is on, a Linux kernel team, and more. The flat hierarchy means that " all of the employees do a lot of work that you typically wouldn't do as a leaf-node employee at a big company ", which includes making company decisions, such as which projects to take on, whether to increase headcount, and how much vacation time there is.

Igalia is a cooperative, so votes are taken on those kinds of questions. " These are not decisions you have any influence at all over at a big company. " One of the nice things about that arrangement is that the people who are making the decision are the ones who are affected by it, which is " just not the case at a standard company ". The most obvious example for that is layoffs, Yang said.

items.title: Any window from your Mac, on your iPhone and iPad
items.summary: Article URL: https://github.com/Saffsanity/sill Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50112739 Points: 139 # Comments: 31
items.content:
Sill shows a window from your Mac, or the whole desktop, on your iPhone or iPad. You use it there with touch, a trackpad, a keyboard or Apple Pencil. Sill for Mac captures the window, encodes it as HEVC video and sends it to the Sill app on your device. Your taps, clicks, scrolls and keys go back to your Mac. Your Mac and your device connect on the same network, over a USB cable, with Direct Wireless Connection when they share no network, or through your own VPN, such as Tailscale, with Remote Access. There is no account and no server in between.

Sill for Mac is a free, notarized download from getsill.app ; with Homebrew , brew install --cask saffsanity/sill/sill installs the same download from Sill's own tap . Sill for iPhone and iPad is free on the App Store , and you can also build it from source (below).

These are the iPad screenshots from the App Store; on iPhone and iPhone Duo, Sill has layouts of its own.

Good to know: Sill shows one window, or the whole desktop, at a time, and it does not play sound from your Mac. The clipboard carries text only, up to 256 KB at a time, and only between apps that both have it. Your Mac needs to be awake, with Sill open. Sill may not be able to wake it. After a restart Sill opens only once someone logs in, with Launch at Login on. Only the iPhones and iPads you paired can connect, unless you turn off Require pairing in Settings › Devices; then any device on your network can, still encrypted. Pairing at home came with Sill for Mac 0.4.0 and Sill for iPhone and iPad 0.5 (2), and each needs the other: the iPhone and iPad app shows an older Sill for Mac as "Update Sill", and an older iPhone and iPad app can't connect to Sill for Mac 0.4.0 or later at home. Since 0.5.1 the two apps share one version number for each release. With Sill for Mac 0.3.1 or earlier, connections on your local network, over the cable and over Direct Wireless Connection are not encrypted, and anything that reaches your Mac there can connect without pairing: update it.

Sill is free, with no ads, no tracking and no subscription. If it is useful to you, a tip through GitHub Sponsors helps pay for the developer account. A tip unlocks nothing: every feature is free.

You need a Mac with Xcode (Sill is built with Xcode 27; the iPhone and iPad app needs Xcode 27.1 or later, for the iPhone Duo's hinge and fold), selected as the active developer directory, with its license accepted.

This builds Sill.app with SwiftPM, signs it with your Apple Development identity, replaces /Applications/Sill.app and opens it. If that was the Sill for Mac you downloaded, grant Screen Recording and Accessibility again and pair each device again: the download keeps its key and paired devices in the data-protection keychain, which only a Developer ID build with the project's provisioning profile reads, and a build of your own keeps them in your login keychain. Without --install it only builds .build/Sill.app . With no Apple Development identity it signs ad hoc, and then Screen Recording and Accessibility have to be granted again after every build.

For work on the host itself, swift run -c release SillHost runs the same host on the command line, with one difference: unless you add --pairing , its home door is plain and open, with no pairing and no encryption, and any device on your network can connect to it, so run it only while developing. The App Store's Sill for iPhone and iPad never dials such a door ("Update Sill"); a Debug build from this repository can ( docs/DEVELOPMENT.md , Pairing at home). With --synthetic it streams a test pattern with no Screen Recording needed.

docs/DEVELOPMENT.md has the rest: every command-line flag, the test tools and the simulator harness, permissions and how to reset them, Remote Access, troubleshooting and releases.

Issues are welcome: bug reports, questions and ideas. For a pull request, keep to the conventions and decisions in CLAUDE.md : Swift and Apple frameworks only, no third-party dependencies, nothing that needs a server, and latency before picture quality. Open an issue before starting anything large. Before a pull request, Tests/checks/run-all.sh runs the same pure checks as CI, in about five minutes and with no device. Contributions are accepted under the project's license. Please report a security problem privately, as SECURITY.md says, not in a public issue.

Sill is licensed under the Apache License 2.0 . Copyright 2026 Noah Saffer.

items.title: Roomba 115, 415, 515 e 575, in promo i robot multifunzione che arrivano dove gli altri si fermano
items.summary: Più bassi e raccolti del Roomba 505, aspirano e lavano sotto letti e divani. Si parte dal 115 con navigazione laser e si arriva al 575, che riconosce gli ostacoli e lava i panni a 75 °C ... Leggi tutto
items.content:
Aspirano, lavano i pavimenti e soprattutto entrano dove un robot più ingombrante resta fuori : sotto il letto, sotto il divano, tra le gambe di sedie e tavoli. Roomba 115, 415, 515 e 575 sono i Roomba multifunzione più piccoli di sempre , fino al 21% più sottili del Roomba Plus 505.

Nessuno dei quattro rinuncia a qualcosa per stare in poco spazio , e salendo di modello si aggiungono la base che lava i panni, l'acqua calda e la visione artificiale.

Il vantaggio della taglia si conta in centimetri. Se il Roomba Plus 505 è alto 10,6 cm, il 415 e il 575 si fermano a 8,35 cm e il 115 a 9,2 cm. Sotto un divano o una rete del letto bastano quei due centimetri per far passare il robot proprio dove la polvere si accumula indisturbata , perché con la scopa non ci arriva nessuno. Anche la pianta si restringe: il 415 misura 29,8 per 30,3 cm, contro i 35,7 per 35,1 cm del 505, e si infila più facilmente tra le gambe di sedie e tavoli.

Tutti e quattro sono Combo, cioè aspirano e lavano il pavimento nella stessa sessione , e tutti si orientano con ClearView LiDAR. È un sensore laser che mappa la casa in meno di dieci minuti , funziona anche con poca luce e fa pulire il robot per file ordinate, stanza dopo stanza, invece che a caso. Quando incontra un tappeto, il robot lo riconosce e non lo bagna.

Le mappe si gestiscono dall'app Roomba Home , dove si programmano le pulizie, si scelgono le stanze e si regola l'intensità su quattro livelli di aspirazione. Il robot risponde anche ai comandi vocali di Alexa, Siri e Google Assistant . Le spazzole in gomma anti-groviglio, infine, non si avvolgono di capelli e peli degli animali.

Il Roomba 115 Combo è la porta d'ingresso della famiglia, e ci entra con 15.000 Pa di aspirazione e l a stessa navigazione laser dei modelli superiori . Per lavare usa un panno in microfibra lavabile fino a 30 volte e il sistema SmartScrub, che strofina con più decisione e pulisce due volte più a fondo .

L'acqua, o il detergente, si dosa su tre livelli . Con una carica copre fino a 84 metri quadrati, memorizza fino a tre mappe per le case su più piani e supera soglie e dislivelli fino a 19 mm .

Chi non vuole nemmeno svuotare il contenitore può sceglierlo con la base AutoEmpty . A fine ciclo il robot ci rientra e la base aspira lo sporco in un sacchetto AllergenLock da 2,5 litri , che trattiene il 99% di pollini e muffe e si sigilla quando lo si estrae, così la polvere non torna nell'aria. Un sacchetto dura fino a tre mesi: in pratica si cambia quattro volte l'anno .

Con il Roomba Plus 415 Combo + AutoWash cambia il modo di lavare, perché al posto del panno singolo arrivano i DualClean, due panni rotanti che girano a 200 giri al minuto e, insieme a SmartScrub, premono sul pavimento per staccare le macchie secche. L'aspirazione sale a 20.000 Pa, e Carpet Boost la aumenta da sola quando il robot passa su un tappeto . In ogni caso, s ui tappeti i panni si sollevano di 10 mm e in modo da lasciare asciutto ciò che non deve essere lavato.

La vera novità è la base AutoWash . Oltre a svuotare il robot nel sacchetto AllergenLock già visto sul 115, lava i panni dopo ogni ciclo e li asciuga con aria calda a 45 °C , così non restano umidi e non fanno cattivo odore.

Ha due serbatoi separati, uno per l'acqua pulita e uno per quella sporca , e un ciclo di autopulizia che risciacqua la base. Il robot torna a lavare con panni puliti e il proprietario se ne occupa una volta ogni tre mesi circa.

Il Roomba 515 Combo + AutoWash porta l'acqua calda nella base AutoWash: dopo ogni ciclo i panni DualClean vengono lavati con acqua calda e poi asciugati a 60 °C . L'aspirazione arriva a 22.000 Pa.

Per parlare del suo secondo punto di forza bisogna "seguire i bordi". Con PerfectEdge la spazzola laterale si allunga e i panni si estendono verso l'esterno , fino dentro gli angoli e lungo i battiscopa, con il 18% di superficie coperta in più. Anche la batteria fa un salto in avanti: fino a 295 minuti di autonomia, abbastanza per circa 185 metri quadrati con una carica. Per gli appartamenti su più livelli le mappe memorizzabili passano da 3 a 5 , e Spot Clean manda il robot su una macchia precisa senza dover rifare tutta la stanza.

Al vertice della famiglia c'è il robot più attento. Il Roomba Plus 575 Combo + AutoWash usa ClearView Pro LiDAR, che costruisce mappe in 3D e rileva gli ostacoli ad altezze diverse, e lo affianca a PrecisionVision AI , una telecamera con riconoscimento delle immagini.

Cavi, calzini e i bisogni dell'animale di casa vengono riconosciuti e aggirati , e non serve più riordinare il pavimento prima di far partire la pulizia. La stessa visione distingue lo sporco secco da quello bagnato e fa ripassare il robot dove serve.

Nella base AutoWash i panni vengono lavati con acqua fino a 75 °C, e poi asciugati con aria calda . L'aspirazione tocca i 25.000 Pa, il valore più alto dei quattro, i panni si estendono di 35 mm verso i bordi e il robot supera soglie fino a 35 mm , quindi passa senza fatica anche soglie particolarmente alte. Tutto questo in un corpo più piccolo del 46%, in volume, rispetto al Roomba Plus 505 Combo.

Per tutto ottobre i quattro robot sono in offerta anche su irobot.it, con spedizione gratuita e due anni di garanzia.

items.title: Thank You, Deno
items.summary: Article URL: https://www.vlt.io/blog/competition-keeps-javascript-moving Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50112331 Points: 74 # Comments: 12
items.content:
Deno is joining Cloudflare & winding down its investment in the runtime. We're all better off because of its existence.

Ryan Dahl announced last week that the Deno team is joining Cloudflare. The Deno runtime winds down over the next year, JSR keeps running on Cloudflare's infrastructure, & the team's new job, per Cloudflare's post , is merging Deno's celld into workerd .

The announcement came two years to the day after Deno 2 shipped. Bun joined Anthropic ten months ago. The tempting conclusion is that the alternative-runtime experiment is over & Node has won by default. In reality, the ecosystem has gotten the benefits Deno was pushing, just not from Deno itself.

Unfortunately, Deno never really hit critical mass in production; Node is as dominant in 2026 as it was in 2018. What Deno did achieve was to reinvigorate & put pressure on the incumbent, & that pressure didn't only run one way.

Deno started as a clean break. Ryan stood up at JSConf EU in 2018 & listed what he'd do differently from Node: deny-by-default permissions, TypeScript as a first-class input, web-standard APIs on the server, ES modules only, a single executable. And, pointedly, no npm , no package.json & no node_modules . Dependencies were URLs. The slides put it plainly: "There is no need to list dependencies."

A lot of us who'd spent years on npm & Node were skeptical of that last part (not the permissions or the TypeScript, which were obviously good) & said so at the time. We'd been there before, in the hotlinking era, when every page pulled jquery.min.js off somebody else's server & broke when it moved or got compromised. A URL tells you where something was, not what it is. Once you care that the bytes you tested are the bytes you ship, you need an integrity hash & somewhere to record it, & you've reinvented the lockfile. Matteo Collina of the Node TSC said in 2020 that "another left-pad incident is waiting to happen, but this time there is no 'central entity' that can fix it." Some of this skepticism was defensive but happened to be right in the end.

Deno 1.0 shipped in 2020 on the original terms, & then spent the next four years walking them back one piece at a time. First the deps.ts convention, one file that re-exported every URL: a manifest in all but name. Then lock.json , an integrity hash per URL: a lockfile. Then import maps, so you could write bare specifiers again. Deno's own documentation today recommends registries over HTTPS imports because they "can drift to different versions across files" & "trust the serving host." Those were the objections from 2018, restated as guidance.

Then Bun showed up. Bun 0.1 was released in July 2022 with the opposite bet: rebuild the toolchain from scratch for speed, but run existing npm packages, read package.json & act as a drop-in replacement for node . About six weeks later, Deno published "Big Changes Ahead for Deno" , announcing npm: specifiers, a commitment to make 80–90% of npm packages work within three months & a new goal of being "the fastest JavaScript runtime." Deno credited user feedback for the shift; the timing suggests Bun was a large part of it. Deno 2 , in October 2024, finished the job with full Node & npm compatibility. Four years after launching as the alternative to Node's ecosystem, Deno had become another way to run it.

That was the right call, & it was also an admission that the ecosystem wasn't going to abandon over a decade's worth of dependencies overnight. Cloudflare's workerd , which it open-sourced in 2022 , grew its own Node compatibility layer for the same reason: that's where the packages are.

Node ended up needing to respond. Since 2018 it has shipped a global fetch , WebSocket , Web Streams & Web Crypto; a stable test runner & --watch ; --env-file & single-executable builds; a stable permission model ; type stripping on by default; node:sqlite ; & require(esm) . Node's contributors (many volunteers) did the hard work to listen & make big changes, & they deserve a ton of credit for it, but I don't think it happens on that timeline without three other runtimes shipping many of these ideas first. A mature open source project rarely lacks good ideas. It lacks urgency, & competitors supply that urgency.

The standards work came out of the same pressure: WinterCG formed in 2022 because several serious runtimes made "what's the minimum common API?" a practical question, & now, as Ecma TC55 , it should outlast whichever runtimes consolidate next.

For most of its history the JavaScript package ecosystem was a monoculture: one client, one registry, & an API contract informal enough that it stayed effectively undocumented for a decade & a half. Nearly every improvement since came from someone refusing to accept the status quo.

Yarn (2016) insisted installs be deterministic & gave us the lockfile, workspaces & an offline cache; npm 5 shipped package-lock.json the next year. pnpm showed that node_modules didn't have to be hundreds of megabytes of duplicated files. Bun made install fast enough that the incumbents had to revisit their performance. Deno argued you should be able to read a dependency's source before you take it, & while URL imports didn't last, that idea did.

The clearest recent example is install scripts. pnpm & Bun stopped running them by default; vlt never did . The argument had been made inside npm for the entire time I worked there without ever becoming the default. In June of this year, after a run of supply-chain worms, GitHub announced that npm 12 would stop running them by default too. Nothing about the idea changed in those years; enough other package managers shipped it that npm could no longer treat it as radical. The pressure runs in both directions too: we borrowed catalogs from pnpm, & pnpm's namedRegistries borrowed our named-registry aliases.

On the registry side, JSR deserves credit. It made a different set of bets than we did: publish TypeScript source, require ESM, generate docs from code. We disagreed with parts of it & added jsr: support to vlt anyway because our users asked for it. It survives the wind-down because, as far as I can tell, it's cheap to run, its API is documented, & Cloudflare had a reason to keep it alive.

The two most popular independent, venture-backed JavaScript runtimes now live inside companies whose business is something else. Jarred Sumner said the Bun team's relationship with the Claude Code team "probably will look similar to the relationship between Google Chrome V8," with more independence, & Cloudflare's post makes clear that workerd's roadmap is Cloudflare's. That's how JavaScriptCore & V8 have always been funded, & it's still a change.

Whether a community fork of the Deno runtime emerges will tell us whether the ecosystem values a secure-by-default, standards-first runtime enough to pay for one that isn't attached to a cloud. And celld-into-workerd is new optionality at a layer that has had very little: a self-hostable, open implementation of Workers & Durable Objects, led by Ryan & Bert Belder.

JavaScript has insurance at almost every layer: three production engines, several runtimes, several package managers. When one layer consolidates, as the runtime layer is doing now, the others hold. The churn that makes this possible is also what people complain about most. "JavaScript fatigue" has been a running joke for a decade: a new framework every week, a new bundler every month, & yet another package manager, which, yes, I'm aware I've contributed to. But nobody had to leave Node to get fetch , a permission model or TypeScript without a build step, & nobody has to switch package managers to get install scripts turned off by default anymore. Those things showed up in the tools people were already using because someone else shipped them first & the incumbent had to answer. The projects didn't always win, but the ideas usually did, & end-users collected them either way.

To Ryan, Bert, Bartek & the rest of the Deno team (past & present): your collective efforts have enriched our shared ecosystem. Thank you!
