items.title: RPKI now protects 70% of internet routes
items.summary: Article URL: https://ipinfo.io/blog/rpki-protects-70-internet-routes Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50112330 Points: 147 # Comments: 42
items.content:
Start using accurate IP data for cybersecurity, compliance, and personalization—no limits, no cost.

The Internet relies on networks telling each other which IP addresses they can deliver traffic to, using BGP (Border Gateway Protocol). These routing announcements have historically depended heavily on trust. When a network announces addresses it shouldn’t, accidentally or deliberately, traffic can be sent to the wrong place and services can become unreachable.

On February 24, 2008, Pakistan Telecom (AS17557) tried to block YouTube inside Pakistan by announcing a more specific route for YouTube's addresses. Its upstream provider, PCCW Global (AS3491), accepted the announcement and passed it to the rest of the Internet, redirecting YouTube traffic to Pakistan globally for roughly two hours ( RIPE NCC's case study ). That’s exactly the kind of error RPKI is designed to prevent. Work on RPKI had started at the IETF two years earlier, and the regional Internet registries began issuing RPKI certificates in 2011.

RPKI (Resource Public Key Infrastructure) lets the holder of a block of IP addresses publish a signed record, a Route Origin Authorization (ROA), naming the networks (Autonomous Systems, or ASes) allowed to announce it. Network operators that check RPKI compare announcements against those records and can reject the ones that fail.

The share of routed prefixes (blocks of IP addresses) that are RPKI-valid rose from 54.0% in September 2025 to 70.3% in September 2026, a gain of 16.4 percentage points, or 30% in a year. That’s a sharp increase. In each of the two years before, it rose three to four points. Much of the jump came from one country: China went from 3.7% of its IPv4 addresses in valid routes to 83.0%, almost 60% of the global gain counted by addresses.

RPKI is doing what it was designed to do. A typical valid prefix is seen by 596 of the routers that feed the public RIPE RIS and RouteViews collectors. One with no RPKI record is seen by 595, and an invalid one by just two.

In August, the Internet Society Pulse found RPKI-related activity accounts for under 1% of daily BGP update volume, a share that is rising but still small, so RPKI is not itself destabilizing routing. We wanted to know whether RPKI was actually protecting Internet routing.

Routes with an RPKI record and routes with none travel equally far: a typical one is seen by 596 and 595 vantage points. Routes that fail the check are seen by just two. Now that enough networks check, they are dropping these invalid routes. Nearly half of all invalid routes reach only a single vantage point. When the wrong network announces the addresses, the clearest kind of hijack or mistake, 71% reach only one.

This changes how country-level RPKI statistics should be read. A country can look bad because of announcements almost nobody sees.

Simply counting invalid routes can badly exaggerate how much of a country is affected. Spain has the highest share of invalid IPv4 prefixes at 28.2%. Count the addresses in those routes instead, weighted by how many vantage points see each one, and it falls to 0.057%. Slovakia falls from 17.4% to almost zero. Italy has the highest figure of any country with at least a million IPv4 addresses, 0.121%, up from 0.075% a year ago, and 90% of it is one network.

WIND TRE (AS1267) announces 34 routes in its own address space that its own ROAs don't allow: 19 are more specific than the ROAs permit, and 15 come from AS1267 while the ROA names WIND TRE's other network, AS24608. None reaches more than 77 vantage points, against about 617 for the signed blocks around them.

Counted by IPv4 addresses on September 28 each year, the share in RPKI-valid routes rose from 42.7% in 2023 to 47.9% in 2024, 53.1% in 2025 and 65.0% in 2026. The last jump was 11.9 points, against about five in each previous year.

Removing China shows how much of that was one country. Outside China, the share rose from 58.0% to 63.2%, a 5.2-point gain, a little less than the year before.

China's own change was extraordinary. 3.7% of its IPv4 addresses were in valid routes in September 2025, and 83.0% a year later. Most of that happened this year: at the end of December 2025, just 2.9% of China's routed prefixes were valid. It also changed which way it moves the world figure. In 2025 China pulled the global average down: 53.1% worldwide against 58.0% without China. In 2026 it pushed it up: 65.0% against 63.2%. Others moved a long way too: Egypt from 23% to 99%, Kazakhstan from 16% to 84%, Mexico from 37% to 78%, and South Africa from 38% to 60%.

Where the unprotected addresses are is just as concentrated. Of all routed IPv4 space not in RPKI-valid routes on September 28, nearly 60% is in the United States, and about one in four addresses belongs to the US Department of Defense (more on who holds IPv4 in an upcoming post). Most of that is space the Department began announcing in 2021 to watch for misuse, not to run services.

In early 2025 there were concerns that IPv6 adoption of RPKI was slowing. Instead, it accelerated and has now overtaken IPv4. In RPKI's 2024 year in review for RIPE Labs, Job Snijders noted IPv6 ROA growth "seems to be stalling." Over our window, IPv6 routed prefixes marked valid rose from 56% to 79% while IPv4 prefixes rose from 54% to 68%, putting IPv6 roughly ten points ahead. The Hurricane Electric RPKI report shows the same ordering.

Two other metrics he flagged also changed: the average number of address blocks per ROA climbed back from 2.31 at the end of December to 2.62, and publication points, which he counted falling from 63 to 53 and read as consolidation, rose from 73 to 91 as more organizations began hosting their own repositories instead of relying on their registry.

RPKI validates who may originate a prefix. It does not validate the path, and it cannot catch an attacker who stays inside the permission you published, so it's not bulletproof.

On August 28, 2026, a route for 162.55.80.0/24 (a block of 256 addresses) appeared with Hetzner's AS24940 forged as the origin. Hetzner's ROA covered the surrounding /16, a block 256 times larger, and allowed announcements as small as a /24, so the forged route satisfied it. The route was RPKI-valid, no legitimate /24 existed to compete with it, and longest-prefix-match meant everyone preferred it. That was enough to obtain a genuine TLS certificate and serve a malicious Virtualizor update to hypervisors, as documented by Kentik . Nothing about RPKI failed. The ROA permitted it.

We measured how common that posture is. Of 855,217 RPKI-covered IPv4 routes, 138,698, or 16.2%, have a ROA looser than the route announced and no more-specific route of their own filling the gap. For IPv6 it is 20.9%. That leaves roughly 18 million more-specific prefixes an attacker could announce today, forge the origin, and come out RPKI-valid and uncontested.

Operators in the same business make very different choices here. Among hosting providers, Contabo has an open window on 540 of 553 covered routes and DigitalOcean on 780 of 863, while OVH sits at 11.5%. Access providers are worse still: Cablevision at 98.1%, Shaw at 96.5%, Bharti Airtel at 85.0%.

RFC 9319 already says the best practice is to leave maxLength unset. maxLength is the setting that lets a ROA also cover smaller blocks inside it, so leaving it unset means a ROA matches only the block actually announced. Hetzner tightened three prefixes after the incident, including the one that was hijacked, though 49 of its 63 covered routes remain open.

RPKI coverage can also disappear without causing an outage. A missing ROA simply removes the protection, and nobody notices unless they look. We found several cases where that happened over the past year.

Unlike China, Mauritius saw its RPKI coverage fall. The share of its IPv4 addresses in valid routes fell from 94.0% to 69.0% between September 2025 and September 2026. SEACOM (AS37100) lost four of its six ROAs on January 1. One covered 105.16.0.0/12, a block of about a million addresses, 46% of which are in Mauritius. That block alone explains Mauritius's drop, and it still had no ROA on September 28.

Two other operators show the same thing happening and then being fixed. Saudi Telecom (AS25019) lost RPKI protection on 19 routes, including six large blocks totaling about 1.6 million addresses, when the ROAs for those six blocks disappeared between March 30 and April 13. Saudi Arabia's coverage recovered when the ROAs came back on September 21 and 22.

In Morocco, Orange Maroc (AS36925) is the only large operator that publishes ROAs, and most of them went missing twice: from July 2025 to July 2026, and again from July 25 to September 3. Morocco went from 20% covered to almost none, and back.

There is a critical measurement trap here. Some validation methods can count an RPKI record as failed even though it is still providing protection in practice.

Every signed record carries a link to the certificate above it. When an operator moves its repository, that link can go stale, and a check that inspects records one by one will report a hard failure. But the validation that actually produces the list routers use never follows that link, it walks down from the trust anchors instead.

items.title: Houthi missile attack on Yemeni presidential palace kills five, minister says
items.summary: Yemen's information minister says the prime minister and other ministers were unhurt when ballistic missiles hit al-Maashiq Palace.
items.content:
Five people have been killed and 16 injured in a Houthi missile attack targeting the presidential palace in the port city of Aden in southern Yemen, which is the seat of the internationally-recognised government, officials say.

Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani told the BBC that the prime minister and other ministers were unhurt when five ballistic missiles hit al-Maashiq Palace.

The Houthis' military spokesman, Yahya Sarea, said they struck "the Saudi enemy's military operations headquarters in Aden".

A coalition led by Saudi Arabia backs the government and is providing air support for an offensive by pro-government forces against the Iran-backed Houthis.

Yemeni health minister Qasim Buhaibeh said the casualties included "those working to guard the site and civilian employees".

The country's Prime Minister Shaya Zindani condemned the Houthis' attack on Aden, calling it "cowardly" and a "continuation of their criminal behaviour".

He said the government continued to carry out its duties and vowed that it would not weaken the resolve of its forces to continue operations against the Houthis on Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast and other front lines.

Earlier, the Houthis denied that they had attacked Saudi Arabia on Thursday, after the coalition said its forces had intercepted a cruise missile in the Medina region, home to one of Islam's holiest shrines.

The Houthis have been launching missiles and drones at airports, oil and gas facilities, and military bases in Saudi Arabia in retaliation for the strikes on the territory that they control in western Yemen, including the capital Sanaa.

On Saturday, a Houthi missile strike killed 13 people at Riyadh's international airport, which was the deadliest attack in Saudi Arabia in more than a decade.

Saudi Arabia's deputy foreign minister accused Iran of encouraging the Houthis to escalate their conflict with the kingdom.

"Iran continues to arm, train and support the Houthi militia in violation of UN Security Council resolutions," Rayed Krimly told reporters, according to AFP news agency.

"We think that the escalation by the Houthis at this latest stage of the conflict is encouraged by Iran," he added.

There was no immediate response from Iran's government. However, it has previously denied supplying weapons to the Houthis and said it only supports them politically.

Iran's foreign minister has also said it is ready to provide "any assistance necessary to facilitate the start of talks" between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis.

Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the internationally-recognised government from Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.

A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.

The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they call a Saudi blockade of their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.

The conflict escalated in September after the Houthis seized part of Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a chokepoint for global shipping. Their advance contributed to a rise in oil prices following six months of war between the US, Israel and Iran.

Last week, pro-government forces said they had regained control of territory overlooking Bab al-Mandab after launching a major counter-offensive with the support of Saudi air strikes.

At least 1,282 people have been killed and 5,890 injured in the fighting in Yemen since 6 August, according to the government's health ministry.

The UN says another 201,000 people have been displaced and that there has been an alarming surge in suspected cholera cases.

items.title: Meta’s new commercial terms will allow the scraping of news sites: experts
items.summary: Article URL: https://www.niemanlab.org/2026/10/metas-new-commercial-terms-will-allow-the-scraping-of-news-sites-legal-experts-say/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50111852 Points: 273 # Comments: 98
items.content:
Meta can use web scrapers to crawl and collect content from websites “associated with” business accounts on its platforms, according to its new commercial terms of use.

The update , set to go into effect on October 30, will include news publishers with business accounts. These accounts allow companies or public figures to manage Facebook pages, Messenger accounts, Instagram profiles, or WhatsApp channels from one place. While journalism isn’t the only industry that will be affected by this update, virtually every news organization has at least one Meta business account, including Nieman Lab.

The new terms broadly cover business accounts that manage pages and groups, run advertisements, push marketing messages, and use the platform’s business account dashboard . As written, the new terms could be used to argue that Meta can scrape content from news sites and use that content to train the company’s AI products, according to three legal experts who reviewed the terms at Nieman Lab’s request.

RELATED ARTICLE “An astonishing theft of unprecedented proportions”: Court records show what Microsoft and OpenAI actually thought about AI training Sarah Scire September 18, 2026 “This is a remarkable provision to bury in [the] terms of service, given that this would give Meta access to material that would likely cost many millions of dollars in a licensing market,” said Matt Topic , a media and intellectual property attorney at Loevy & Loevy. “It’s not clear whether a court would enforce this, but publishers should assume that it would be enforceable.”

In early October, Meta alerted users to the update in a blog post and on the Meta Business Suite. The updated terms explicitly state that Meta can use the content it collects from associated websites to “train” Meta products. Elsewhere in its terms of service, the company defines “AI at Meta” as one of those products.

You authorize us (or any entity acting on our behalf) to use automated software (such as web scrapers, bots, robots, spiders, crawlers, and user agents) and create test credentials to access, index, cache, analyze, collect, retrieve, or crawl the domains, web pages, or URLs (and any content available through them) that are associated with your products or services, or that are made available through your or users’ use of Meta Company Products and services, and to periodically pull updates from such domains, web pages, or URLs. Meta may use any content from such domains, web pages, or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain the integrity of, the Meta Company Products, services, and features provided under these Commercial Terms and any other applicable supplemental terms.

“For news publishers, this clearly represents permission to Meta to train AI on any content from their sites and possibly to deploy some of that content, even in competition with the publishers themselves,” said James Grimmelmann , a professor of digital and information law at Cornell Law School. “On the broadest possible interpretation, this would be used to develop a comprehensive archive of all content that Meta would then serve as it wanted to directly or through AI.”

Currently, there is no option for business accounts to opt out of these new terms ahead of October 30. The update reads, “If you do not agree to the updated terms, please stop all access or use of our Products for business or commercial purposes.”

In short, “publishers either have to trust that Meta doesn’t mean the full extent of what these terms say, or they have to stop [using business accounts],” said Grimmelmann.

Meta declined to answer a list of questions about these updated terms. A public affairs spokesperson at the company said in an email that language around crawling was previously scattered across different terms of use, including terms about using generative AI in ads , and this update consolidates them in one place. He also said that the new terms will not change how Meta crawls publishers in the future, and that “content owners can still manage how their content is accessed by using robots.txt.”

On its developer page , Meta currently has instructions for how to block its crawlers using robots.txt, a file that tells bots which parts of a website they can and cannot access.

However, legal experts said the new language creates an opening for Meta to argue its commercial terms supersede other blocking instructions. The update also states that Meta can create “test credentials” in order to scrape websites associated with business accounts. Grimmelmann said this would technically allow Meta to “sign up as a fake user” to bypass registration walls on a publisher’s site to access content. Meta declined to answer Nieman Lab’s questions about whether the “test credentials” would bypass paywalls or other paid content.

RELATED ARTICLE Federal appeals court upholds Thomson Reuters’ landmark AI copyright win Andrew Deck September 30, 2026 Any attempt to train Meta’s AI products with content collected under these new terms would still hinge on unsettled legal questions about AI training and fair use, legal experts said. Several lawsuits between publishers and AI developers are currently winding their way through federal courts. That includes a class-action suit filed in May by five large book publishers, alleging Meta pirated millions of books in order to train its Llama large language models (LLMs).

Meta’s decision to tether access to its business products to broad scraping permissions echoes a concept in antitrust law called “tying,” according to Benjamin Sobel , a law professor at the University of Wisconsin. “If you want to use the Meta products that require acceptance of the commercial terms, you have to also acquiesce to the scraping and crawling permissions exacted in those terms.”

Sobel compared the move to Google’s recent policies around its AI search products. In order to appear in Google’s traditional search results, publishers now have to consent to their content also being used in AI Overviews and AI Mode .

Meta’s new commercial terms come on the heels of the company’s rollout of its paid subscription service, Meta One . The cash-for-links program restricts the number of external links that some accounts on Facebook and Instagram can post without subscribing. Put another way, Meta has begun charging users to post links to the same content that it will be permitted to crawl for free. Earlier this month, Press Gazette reported that some news publishers are currently exempt from the link limit. Meta declined to answer Nieman Lab’s question about the service.

RELATED ARTICLE Meet the journalists training AI models for Meta and OpenAI Andrew Deck February 20, 2025 Nieman Lab first learned about Meta’s new commercial terms through a reader tip. Stephen Beale, the founder and editor of The Steampunk Explorer, got in touch when he saw a notice of the upcoming change in his Meta Business Suite dashboard.

“Traditionally, you have this idea that Meta might be using content [posted] on Facebook or Instagram for training,” Beale told Nieman Lab. “But this was different because they’re saying that [since you are] a business user of Facebook, they have the right to go out and grab information from basically wherever you have a presence.”

Beale has long depended on Facebook as a way to connect with his audience and refer traffic to his site. Fans of steampunk — a retrofuturistic subgenre of science fiction — skew older, he said, and the community is “totally entrenched on Facebook.” For many, their only interactions with the community happen on Facebook or at in-person events that they learned about on Facebook.

Beale said he’s seriously considering shutting down his accounts before October 30.

“I know my site has been scraped to death,” he said. “But it just seems like such an arrogant, in-your-face move on [Meta’s] part… It just makes me angry and I don’t want them to get away with it.”

Are you considering changing how you use Meta-owned platforms? Let us know at [email protected] .

items.title: Tip-off foiled US teen suspect's plot to attack Hindu temple, police say
items.summary: The alleged plot only failed because the 19-year-old suspect's gun jammed outside the place of worship, say police.
items.content:
A Taco Bell cashier's alleged plot for a mass shooting at a Hindu temple near Chicago was thwarted by a tip-off from one of his colleagues, investigators say.

Alexandros Paporakis, 19, from Palatine, Illinois, appeared in court on Wednesday charged with one count of making a terrorist threat and one count of unlawful possession of a weapon.

Paporakis allegedly sent a message about the planned attack on Sunday to the co-worker, who alerted authorities, officials said.

Police said they found writings in which Paporakis identified as a white supremacist and wrote about his hatred for non-white people.

Palatine police chief William Nord said on Thursday they were notified about a mass shooting plot on Sunday by someone who had received "concerning electronic communications" from Paporakis.

"These communications played a vital role in bringing this matter to the attention of law enforcement," said the police chief.

According to CBS, the BBC's US partner, prosecutors said the tipster had worked with Paporakis.

Nord said a red Honda RDX registered to Paporakis entered the car park of a "known Hindu temple" in the suburb of Aurora at Sunday lunchtime.

The suspect allegedly tried to open fire, but the gun jammed, so he drove home, where he lived with his mother.

According to NBC Chicago, Paporakis told his colleague over phone messages that his gun had jammed and he got out of there "super-fast".

Once home, he "searched internet trying to learn how to unjam his gun & called a colleague informing them of [his] intent to carry out a mass shooting", reports NBC Chicago.

The police chief said officers had searched Paporakis' home, where they found a rifle, loaded magazines, hundreds of rounds of rifle ammunition and body armour.

Nord said they also discovered an eight-page document by the suspect containing "extremist ideologies" and revealing his plans for an attack.

In the writings, he described himself as a "sociopathic white supremacist neo-Nazi", according to CBS.

Police have questioned Paporakis' mother, who was said to be unco-operative.

The Hindu temple identified by local media as the intended target said it had implemented new security measures.

India's Ministry of External Affairs said the incident "adds to growing concerns over racist hostility and anti-India hate in the US".

US congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi of Illinois said he was "horrified" by the incident.

In a Facebook statement, he said he and his family worship at the temple and were there last Sunday.

The Chicago metropolitan area is home to one of the biggest Indian-American populations in the US.

items.title: Are student protests being manipulated ahead of France's presidential election?
items.summary: France's prime minister has suggested that student anger is being weaponised, as the unions and other protesters prepare to take to the streets too.
items.content:
Over the last few years, we have regularly witnessed farmers angry about costly regulations lobbing manure at local mayoral offices, while masked youths periodically hurl homemade grenades at riot police in disadvantaged city suburbs.

For over three weeks now, thousands of students have barricaded entry to high schools and taken their grievances to the streets.

This Saturday, hundreds of new demonstrations have been announced across France.

Students are expected to be joined by workers' unions and key figures from the so-called "yellow vest" movement.

France's prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, suggested this week that student anger was being manipulated as politics heats up ahead of next year's presidential election.

The gilets jaunes (yellow vests) demonstrated against cost-of-living hikes for over a year from 2018 - becoming one of the longest-lived protest movements in French history.

Jérôme Rodrigues, a prominent gilets jaunes activist, has used Instagram to encourage people to join Saturday's demonstrations.

The protests should give a voice to those who "want to be able to live decently, no longer have to count every cent, and no longer have to choose between eating and driving", he said in a video.

"Anger has no political party. An empty fridge has no political party," he added.

Social unrest, government borrowing costs at eye-watering highs, a deeply divided French parliament and an apparent revolving door of exasperated French prime ministers - six prime ministers over the last five years - all claiming to want to reduce their country's public debt.

Is France at breaking-point - and what does this all mean for the eurozone currency the French are such a huge part of?

"You can't compare France to the Greece debt crisis of 2012 or Argentina in 2001. And the financial markets know it," economist Anne-Laure Delatte told me.

She is a CNRS Tenured Researcher at the Economics Department of Paris Dauphine University; a well-known face in debates on French media on the parlous state of the country's public debt.

"The markets recognised already in 2024 that we would have a budgetary problem after [snap] elections left parliament deeply divided between three [opposing political] blocs but they also realise France is a big country with the ability to raise taxes if necessary."

"Our situation is more like the UK in 2023 with Liz Truss," suggests Delatte, referring to the then UK prime minister's so-called mini budget, which triggered a sharp drop in the pound, a spike in government bond yields and soaring mortgage rates.

"The crisis was relatively short-lived because the markets recognised the UK had the financial tools to right itself."

"Here in France it would be painful, but a 4% increase in VAT would raise the 120bn euros needed to plug government debt. Investors know that," she concludes.

Maybe, in theory. And, as Delatte also points out, the European Central Bank would likely intervene if France's finances nosedived to the point where other European economies would be affected.

But with so many French citizens already visibly unhappy with the status quo, imagine the reaction if taxes were to increase, or welfare and education budgets decrease, further.

France's national motto is liberté, égalité, fraternité (freedom, equality and fraternity), but that is certainly not the sense you get on seething streets and in viral social media posts.

I met 17-year-olds Maxime, Madeleine and Elodie this week, perched on big green dustbins that have been used to block the entrance to their high school as part of the weeks' long protest.

They told me things were bad enough here, in the 3rd district of Paris, with holes in classroom walls, swelling class sizes and a dearth of teaching staff, but the teenagers were more than aware, they said, that the situation was far worse in their capital city's disadvantaged suburbs.

"France likes to speak of égalité ," they told me "but the reality is the poor here are prejudiced against, while the rich benefit."

None of them will be old enough to vote in the presidential election in France next spring but they questioned whether the changing face of politicians in power made all that much difference anyway.

The three young women told me large-scale protests seemed the only way to get heard by French authorities.

'Everyone hates the police' – what France's school protests reveal about a divided nation

France halts use of stun grenades after boy's hand blown off in student protests

Cultural icon Victor Hugo, the 19th-Century author of French Revolution classic Les Misérables , also an activist for the French Republic, proclaimed: " Si vous n'êtes pas contents, manifestez, criez, hurlez, mais ne subissez pas ."

("If you are not happy, protest, shout, scream but do not give up and give in.")

Amongst crowds of protesting students walking through Paris on Thursday, I came across a number of mums, with placards around their necks, reading: "Mums in solidarity."

Were they there to protest or to protect their kids, I asked? "Both!" was the emphatic response.

Gwen, 37, said she and other mothers were taking it in turns every morning to co-ordinate between students and police at their local school lock-in.

This came after mounting accusations of police brutality, denied by France's interior ministry, during protests earlier this month in which hundreds were injured and a 15-year-old boy in the town of Lens lost a hand.

France's interior minister has since suspended the use of stun grenades by police at high school demonstrations.

Gwen told me she did not mind that her son was missing weeks of school as a result of the lock-ins. "It's a far better education for him to wake up to his civic duty and to fight for what is just in society," she said.

At Thursday's demo I also came across 17-year-old Lola and her mother, Sandrine, sharing a placard that said revolution was the most beautiful expression of humanity.

"My mum took to the streets in '68," Lola said proudly. "Now it's my turn. No point in waiting for the presidential election in France. We want change now."

Student protests in Paris in May 1968 are the stuff of legend in France. Demands for better education inspired workers to join the marches which turned into the ­biggest general strike in French ­history. It set the standard for revolutionary upheaval for a generation and is credited with creating new opportunities for the French left.

Now, though, with six months to go before an already fraught presidential election in France, there are accusations that the hard left, under presidential hopeful Jean-Luc Mélenchon, is weaponising student frustration.

"Members of [Mélenchon's] France Insoumise (LFI) are instrumentalising the high school movement for their electoral advantage," said Sébastien Lecornu on Wednesday. He accused them of encouraging protests, then going through the motions of condemning any violence.

But "Mélenchon for President!" is a chant you often hear amongst the students in the streets.

Supporters applaud his desire for a wealth tax in France, for lowering the voting age to 16 and for being the only presidential candidate to turn up to French schools to examine the state of them, several demonstrators told me.

For Marine Le Pen, the nationalist anti-immigration favourite in France's presidential race, the solution is cutting the country's €11bn contribution to the EU's budget.

There is, though, reason to doubt that any new French president, from the left or the right, will be able to break the impasse over France's finances.

France is far from alone in Europe right now faced with an ageing population, a generous welfare state to run and a national economy squeezed by outside pressures such as US President Donald Trump's trade tariffs and the war in the Persian Gulf.

Whether in France, Germany, Sweden or Italy, there is an inherent tension between politicians who hesitate to tell voters the truth about shrinking public finances, the defence establishment's demand for higher defence spending and citizens' insistence on improved public services.

In France, that pressure is particularly acute. French public expenditure, at about 57% GDP, is one of the steepest amongst wealthy nations worldwide.

Social spending, particularly on pensions, is exceptionally large, while French citizens pay one of the highest overall tax and social contribution burdens in Europe. Simply put, they expect a welfare and public service bang for their buck.

But economist Anne-Laure Delatte does not believe having a new president will ease her country's financial migraine.

"We need constitutional change. A new system. A new Republic," she told me.

"Our Fifth Republic is centred around a powerful president. Parliament is there to block him or her rather than to find consensus or to make new laws."

The French parliamentary election that follows the 2027 presidential vote is likely to be as divided as ever, she believes: "We need a system where MPs have more power and should learn consensus and coalition-building from our European neighbours."

items.title: BeBox is a Haiku application that emulates Be Inc.'s BeBox
items.summary: Article URL: https://github.com/johnrash/bebox Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50111742 Points: 59 # Comments: 14
items.content:
BeBox is a Haiku application that emulates Be Inc.'s BeBox, the dual-processor computer that BeOS was born on. It runs both PowerPC models from their original boot ROMs, with BeOS for PowerPC from Developer Release 6 through R5.0.3. It also runs the Hobbit prototypes that came before them, built around two AT&T Hobbit processors, with Be's 1993-94 system from their surviving disks.

The window shows the emulated screen between the two front panel LED columns (the "blinkenlights"), sixteen light pipe segments each: a CPU load bar of fifteen LEDs over the power LED (left) or the disk LED (right), lime and amber like the real ones (or red and green, if you prefer).

Not emulated yet: the parallel port, GeekPort, MIDI and infrared ports.

Changes to the hardware restart the machine. A device type set without a file is turned back into "None" when the preferences are saved.

Before the PowerPC BeBox, Be built its machine around two AT&T 92010 "Hobbit" processors, three AT&T DSP3210 signal processors and the BeBus. A few prototypes survive with their disks, running Be's 1993-94 system: a window server, a console, the Browser and its dock.

Not emulated: the three DSPs and what hangs off them (sound, the telephone and modem), the Ethernet card, the joystick controller and the parallel port. The system starts without them (its sound server reports an error).

No boot ROM of these machines survives, so BeBox does the boot ROM's job: it loads /system/kernel from the boot volume (the floppy if one is inserted, else the SCSI disk with the lowest ID) and starts it. To run one:

The installer floppy and disks 1of7 to 7of7 install the November 1994 system (the one on the "pixels" disk) on a new disk. The installer floppy has no window of its own: its /system/Browser copies a minimal system (kernel, servers, shell, /Installer ) from the floppy to the first hard disk, without asking and without showing anything but the pointer. Boot it only with the disk to install on: it replaces the system files of any other Hobbit disk it finds.

Each release likes a machine of its own (its boot ROM, its disks, maybe the 133 MHz model), so the machine is kept in a profile : everything in the preferences except Keyboard & mouse and the LED look, plus the boot ROM flash (with the boot ROM updates BeOS installs) and the NVRAM (with the boot volume). Machine > Profile lists the profiles to switch between (a running BeBox restarts with the other one), and has New profile... (a copy of the current profile, under a name like "BeOS5 133 MHz" or "DR8 66 32 MB"), Rename and Delete . The status line shows the current profile. Profiles are folders in ~/config/settings/BeBox/Profiles/ ; the settings from before profiles became the profile "Default".

"-" means not tried yet. The DR8.2 image is a Mac updater, and the R4 image is x86 only. The boot ROM from the R3 CD works with every release tested here, so one profile with it can run them all.

DR6 predates the 1.1d7 boot ROM: BeBox hands its kernel the PCI device table in the older format it expects. Install it as the CD says: boot the CD, run the Installer from the dock, format the SCSI disk ("Format:" in the left pop-up menu), then install onto it and make it the startup disk. DR6's mouse driver moves the pointer twice as far left and down as right and up (that is DR6, not the emulation). The Developer Releases' date prints the year as years since 1900 (126 for 2026).

In Preferences > Network , turn on the Ethernet card (port 300h, IRQ 5 by default, as Be's software expects). In BeOS's Network preferences, add a "Novell NE2000 compatible adapter (ISA)" with the same port and IRQ, and choose DHCP (R4.5) or set IP 10.0.2.15, mask 255.255.255.0, gateway 10.0.2.2 and DNS 10.0.2.3 by hand. The host is 10.0.2.2 from the BeBox. Forwarded host ports ( tcp:2121:21, tcp:2323:23 ) make services running in BeOS reachable from the host.

In Preferences > Storage , make a SCSI ID a Shared folder and choose a Haiku folder. At power on BeBox copies the folder, with its attributes (file types, icons), to a fresh BFS volume that BeOS mounts like any disk; the releases with BFS (Advanced Access and later) can use it. When BeOS has shut down (Be menu > Shut Down) and the BeBox is powered off, BeOS's changes go back to the folder: new and changed files, attributes, deletions. A file changed on both sides meanwhile keeps the Haiku version, and BeOS's is saved next to it as "NAME (BeBox)". If BeOS did not shut down cleanly, the volume is kept and given back to BeOS at the next power on, so that it can repair it first. As the whole folder is copied at every power on, keep it small.

Hard disks are raw images or QCOW2 images, which only take the space that is written (thin provisioning) and can be overlays of a backing image. bebox-img manages them, and reads files from BeOS volumes (BFS) and from the Hobbit prototypes' disks:

For example bebox-img extract "BeOS Release 3 PowerPC.iso" /beos/etc/bebox_bootmain.image r3.rom .

On a Hobbit disk, extract also copies whole directories ( / for the whole disk) into a new folder, keeping the files' dates, and ls shows the files' types and creators: bebox-img extract hobbit-930800009.img / pixels . No BeOS release reads the Hobbit's file system (DR6 to DR8 have a later, incompatible version of it, the others BFS), so this is the way to its files: extract them, then give the folder to a BFS release as a shared folder . The Hobbit's programs do not run on the PowerPC; its sources, headers, text and pictures are what is useful.

Also get Mips , get EmulatedTime , get DiskLed , get AudioStats (the sound output's counters: underruns are gaps), get Profiles , get Profile and set Profile (switches, restarting a running machine), and the commands pwon , pwof , rset and cadl (Ctrl+Alt+Delete). Replies come after the action.

BeBox [--profile NAME] [--rom-dir DIR] [--boot-rom IMAGE] [--model 66|133|hobbit] [--kernel FILE] [--ram MB] [--video s3|cirrus] [--scsiN-disk FILE] [--scsiN-cd FILE] [--scsiN-share FOLDER] [--ide0 FILE] [--floppy FILE] [--net] [--net-forward SPEC] [--power-on] sets up the machine (the settings are kept). --profile switches to a profile first, making it as a copy of the current one if there is none; the other options change that profile.

bebox-headless runs a machine without a window, for tests and debugging: serial ports to files or TCP, scripted keys and mouse clicks, screenshots, instruction traces, memory dumps and watches. bebox-headless --help lists the options.

On Haiku (with haiku_devel , zlib_devel and libslirp_devel ): make builds the app; package/build-package.sh builds the app and the tools and creates the package.

MIT, see LICENSE . The application icon ( artwork/BeBox.hvif ) is by zuMi, under the MIT License. The icons in artwork/icons come from Haiku's icon set (MIT, Haiku, Inc.). The BeBox ROMs and BeOS are not part of this project.

items.title: Letters with 'suspicious substances' sent to US senators and election offices
items.summary: A number of states have confirmed they were targeted by the mailings, including Oklahoma, Ohio and Louisiana.
items.content:
Federal authorities say they are investigating "potentially hazardous" letters containing "suspicious substances" that have been sent to congressional and state election offices around the US.

The FBI and the US Postal Inspection Service (USPIS) said they were trying to trace the "suspicious mailings", some of which were intercepted before they were received.

Authorities declined to say how many offices had been targeted, but several secretaries of state and congressional offices reported receiving the letters.

Coming just weeks before the US midterm elections, it echoes previous security scares involving suspicious mail.

The suspicious letters were sent to at least five Democratic senators' offices, most of which were intercepted before delivery.

They include California's Alex Padilla, Connecticut's Chris Murphy and New York's Kirsten Gillibrand, the senators' offices confirmed to the BBC.

New York Senator Chuck Schumer and Delaware Senator Lisa Blunt Rochester were also sent the suspicious pieces of mail, according to the BBC's US partner CBS News.

"This incident is a stark reminder of the very real danger facing those who serve the public and who help administer our elections in the face of increasingly hostile political rhetoric," Padilla said in a statement to the BBC.

Several state offices have also received the suspicious mailings.

Delaware's Department of Elections said its office received and opened a letter containing a white powdery substance on Thursday, adding that staff followed security protocols on handling suspicious mail.

The Oklahoma State Election Board and the Louisiana secretary of state both said this week that their offices had received letters containing a white powder.

The Louisiana office was evacuated after a staff member opened the package on Tuesday, but it has since reopened after law enforcement found no evidence of harmful substances.

Ohio Secretary of State Frank LaRose said his office was the intended recipient of a letter containing white powder, but the USPIS had intercepted it.

The New York State Capitol in Albany and the Wyoming State Capitol in Cheyenne also received suspicious packages, according to emergency responder scanner feed reviewed by the BBC.

"This FBI and the US Postal Inspection Service will continue to safeguard the public and secure elections for American citizens," the agencies said in a statement on Thursday.

The suspicious mailings come just weeks before election day, which will determine the balance of power in Congress.

Ahead of the 2024 election, vote officials in 17 states received suspicious packages .

A year earlier, suspicious envelopes, some laced with fentanyl, were sent to election offices in at least five states.

items.title: Bus hits train stopped on French side of Channel Tunnel, with 19 injured
items.summary: Two people were airlifted to hospital but no-one's life appeared to be in danger, officials said.
items.content:
A bus has hit a stationary freight train near the French entrance to the Channel Tunnel, injuring the driver and 18 passengers, French authorities say.

The bus, which was carrying lorry drivers due to take a shuttle rail service, struck the train at the loading platform of the tunnel in Coquelles, near Calais, at 19:27 (18:27 BST) on Thursday.

The bus driver and one passenger were severely injured and evacuated by helicopter. None of the injuries were life threatening, a local official said.

Local sub-prefect Agathe Cury said freight and Eurostar passenger traffic through the tunnel had not been disrupted after a brief stoppage to evacuate injured people. An investigation has begun.

"Two trains were on either side of the platform. One was being loaded by heavy goods vehicles ahead of a cross-Channel journey, and another train that had previously been loaded was departing," Cury said.

"For a reason that currently remains unknown, the minibus collided with the departing train.

"The bus did not overturn, it is still upright – but the shock and the collision caused injuries to the people involved."

The incident involved a minibus transporting workers who were about to board Le Shuttle. All were men of different nationalities, she added.

It is not clear whether any British nationals are among the injured.

Cury said it was "the first time an incident of this type has occurred" on an Eurotunnel loading platform.

The BBC's Evan Davis, who was travelling through the Eurotunnel to Calais at the time of the incident, witnessed blue light vehicles "concentrated on one of the platforms" as he entered France.

"There were plenty of cars queueing up at check-in when I drove past just now, and I saw some cars going through check-in, so despite the collision they weren't being held," he said from the scene.

Photos published by local French newspaper La Voix du Nord , external showed a small bus with damage to its front and side standing alongside a train, among a crowd of emergency workers.

Eurostar has released an update saying: "An incident occurred several kilometers away from the Channel Tunnel.

"This incident does not involved or impact Eurostar trains running from and to London. All of Eurostar trains will run as expected."

The Eurotunnel runs under the sea between England and France, from Folkestone in Kent to Coquelles on the French side.

Three different rail services operate through the tunnel - the Eurostar, a passenger train that begins in London and goes to several European destinations, freight trains which transport goods and Le Shuttle, which transports vehicles.

items.title: Ucraina, Zelensky sfida Trump e riprende i raid sulle raffinerie russe
items.summary: Starlink riparte ma Musk attacca: 'Il leader ucraino se ne vada'. Kiev resta senza Patriot
items.content:
La pazienza di Kiev è finita. Volodymyr Zelensky ha annunciato la ripresa degli attacchi alle raffinerie russe, sfidando l'annuncio a sorpresa di una tregua energetica da parte di Donald Trump dopo averla rispettata per alcuni giorni accusando Mosca di averla violata. Un'accusa reciproca su una tregua che in realtà nessuno dei due Paesi ha confermato di aver negoziato. Sebbene Trump l'abbia descritta come un impegno che riguarda entrambi i Paesi, i suoi strali si sono concentrati su Zelensky, sollecitato ad andarsene, e sugli attacchi ucraini, responsabili a suo avviso di accentuare la crisi del diesel anche in Usa, compromettendo così le chances dei repubblicani alle Midterm.

Il presidente ucraino rischia così di aggravare la più grave frattura tra Kiev e Washington dall'inizio del conflitto, segnata da una serie di circostanze allarmanti: l'esaurimento dei Patriot, l'interruzione di Starshield (la versione militare di Starlink) poi ripreso ma in modo limitato, il blocco dell'intelligence, il tentativo Usa di sbloccare alcuni asset russi congelati in Europa (stoppato per ora dagli europei).

Nonostante i suoi aiuti, il vecchio continente non dispone di alternative immediatamente disponibili né a Starlink né ai sistemi satellitari americani usati per individuare i lanci di missili russi. Difficile anche reperire Patriot. In compenso Londra ha iniziato ad inviare a Kiev altri missili a lungo raggio Storm Shadow.

"Il divieto (di colpire le raffinerie) è revocato. È finita. Basta così", ha dichiarato uno spazientito Zelensky al Financial Times, mentre Mosca denunciava un raid ucraino su una raffineria nella regione di Rjazan, a sud-est di Mosca: un impianto della compagnia petrolifera statale Rosneft che rappresenta quasi il 5% della capacità di raffinazione russa. Abbattuti anche sei bombardieri russi Su-34M all'aeroporto militare di Borisoglebsk, nella regione di Voronezh. Il leader ucraino, che ha accusato Trump di avere un'affinità istintiva per gli autocrati, ha inoltre chiarito di ritenere che le modifiche alle capacità dei ricevitori Starlink destinati all'uso militare siano state una decisione politica. "Non è stato un problema tecnico, è stata una questione di volontà", ha dichiarato sempre al Financial Times.

Elon Musk ha scaricato la responsabilità su Trump, sostenendo che "i sistemi Starshield sono di proprietà del governo statunitense e sono sotto il suo controllo. Qualsiasi limitazione della velocità o dell'utilizzo viene decisa dalle forze armate statunitensi e, in ultima istanza, dal Potus", ossia dal presidente degli Stati Uniti. "Questo massacro continuerà. È ora che Zelensky se ne vada", ha quindi aggiunto, rincarando il recente monito del commander in chief. Intanto una fonte del ministero della Difesa ucraino ha annunciato che i ricevitori Starlink hanno ripreso a funzionare in fase di movimento, ma soltanto a velocità fino a 100 miglia orarie, pari a circa 160 km/h, una velocità considerata troppo bassa per le missioni d'attacco a medio raggio e per gli intercettori contro i droni russi. Negli ultimi giorni, inoltre, funzionari ucraini hanno riferito di non aver ricevuto dai consueti alleati occidentali gli avvisi sull'arrivo di missili russi, che si basano su sistemi satellitari Usa di rilevamento. Trump ha negato di aver trattenuto informazioni di intelligence e Zelensky ha riferito che la mancata trasmissione degli avvisi è stata presentata a Kiev come un problema tecnico.

"Da ieri, la Russia ha lanciato più di 850 droni Shahed contro l'Ucraina, ci sono ondate continue, e non c'è stata un' ora in cui il nostro cielo sia stato libero da esse", ha denunciato Zelensky, sostenendo che Mosca si sente incoraggiata dai segnali americani. Il bilancio quotidiano delle vittime civili parla di tre morti a Kropyvnytskyi, altri due vicino a Dnipro e tre feriti in un negozio ad Odessa. Questo mentre la Russia ha quasi completato in sole sei settimane la costruzione di una nuova importante base per il lancio di droni a reazione nella regione di Rostov, grande quanto 126 campi da calcio.

Intanto la guerra dei droni tra Russia e Ucraina arriva anche in acque Nato: la Romania ha denunciato la scomparsa di sette persone in seguito a due attacchi con droni contro imbarcazioni nel Mar Nero, dove di recente diverse navi sono state colpite al largo delle coste della Romania e della vicina Bulgaria.

items.title: Trump caccia anche l'inviato Paolo Zampolli
items.summary: Lui lo ringrazia: 'Incarico da un anno e già prorogato. Il presidente ha sempre ragione'
items.content:
Donald Trump caccia anche Paolo Zampolli, suo amico e inviato speciale per le partnership globali. "Gli è stato notificato oggi", hanno detto alcune fonti ad Abc. E poco dopo è arrivato il commento del diretto interessato. "Gli incarichi di inviato speciale hanno una durata di un anno. Trump lo ha prorogato per oltre sei mesi", ha spiegato Zampolli ringraziando il presidente per avergli consentito di servire gli Stati Uniti.

Trump "ha sempre ragione", ha aggiunto riferendosi al fatto che negli anni gli ha sempre dato i consigli giusti. "Anni fa mi fece entrare nel settore immobiliare. Ora mi ha chiesto: 'Perché vuoi lavorare per la pubblica amministrazione quando potresti concludere tutti questi affari?', ha raccontato Zampolli su X. "Ora è il momento di un nuovo capitolo", ha affermato. L'ex inviato speciale nei mesi scorsi aveva suggerito che l'Italia fosse ammessa al Mondiale 2026 al posto dell'Iran e si è descritto come amico del presidente del Movimento cinque stelle Giuseppe Conte. Ma, all'interno del Dipartimento di Stato, Zampolli da mesi era alle prese con un braccio di ferro con il vice segretario di Stato Christopher Landau. Secondo quanto riportato da Politico, i due per mesi si sono scambiati e-mail infuocate in seguito a un disaccordo in merito alla catena di comando. Nelle missive Landau ha esortato Zampolli a limitarsi al proprio ambito di competenza, ovvero le questioni culturali. Inviti che hanno portato ad accesi litigi e accuse prive di riscontri. "Le ordino, ancora una volta, di cessare immediatamente qualsiasi attività su questioni che non siano direttamente legate alla diplomazia culturale", gli ha scritto Landau in un messaggio del 14 novembre 2025. "È evidente che ha un problema con me. Quello che sta facendo è fuori controllo, io ricopro questo incarico su mandato del Presidente degli Stati Uniti d'America. L'unica persona che può affidarmi questo ruolo e che può revocarmi l'incarico è il Presidente degli Stati Uniti", ha spiegato Zampolli a Politico. Una revoca che è ora arrivata. Per il Dipartimento di Stato si tratta di una seconda brusca uscita nell'arco di pochi giorni dopo quella di Kimberly Guilfoyle, l'ambasciatrice americana in Grecia ed ex di Don Jr, costretta a dimettersi su pressione della Casa Bianca. Guilfoyle è stata travolta da accuse di corruzione proprio mentre il segretario di Stato Marco Rubio era ad Atene, offuscando la visita e facendolo infuriare.

items.title: Trump rimuove l'inviato speciale Paolo Zampolli
items.summary: Poche ore prima un articolo di Politico ricostruiva la faida con il vice segretario di Stato Christopher Landau
items.content:
Il presidente americano Donald Trump ha rimosso Paolo Zampolli dal suo incarico di Inviato speciale degli Stati Uniti per le partnership globali. Il controverso amico del presidente Usa è stato licenziato poche ore dopo la pubblicazione, da parte di Politico, di un articolo che ricostruiva la faida, durata mesi e combattuta via email, con il vice segretario di Stato Christopher Landau . Un funzionario americano ha confermato il licenziamento di Zampolli, dichiarando che "il suo incarico di inviato è stato revocato e che non è più un dipendente del governo".

I due funzionari avevano litigato sulle rispettive competenze e sulla catena di comando. Secondo quanto ha ricostruito Politico, Zampolli si sarebbe spinto ben oltre i limitati del suo mandato, incontrando funzionari stranieri per discutere questioni estranee alla cultura. Landau lo avrebbe quindi accusato di “insubordinazione”, mentre Zampolli lo ha attaccato duramente in un’intervista sostenendo che il vice segretario stesse cercando di "distruggere" quello che faceva.

“Gli incarichi di Inviato Speciale durano un anno. Il Presidente Trump lo ha prorogato di oltre sei mesi - ha scritto Zampolli su X - sono profondamente grato al Presidente Trump, al Segretario Rubio e a tutta la squadra. Servire lui e gli Stati Uniti è stato il più grande onore della mia vita. Ora è tempo di un nuovo capitolo: tornare al lavoro, costruire relazioni e concludere affari”.

Special Envoys appointments are for one year. President Trump extended it for more than six months. Years ago, he told me I was too good for modeling and brought me into real estate. Now he told me: “Why do you want to work in government when you can close all these deals?” The President is always right. Serving him and the United States has been the greatest honor of my life. I am deeply grateful to President Trump, Secretary Rubio and the entire team. Now it is time for the next chapter - back to business, building relationships and closing deals. President Trump changed my life once. He just did it again. @POTUS @SecRubio

L'imprenditore è un amico di lunga data di Donald Trump ed è la persona che ha presentato al tycoon la moglie Melania, quando lavorava come agente nel mondo della moda negli anni Novanta e rappresentava la first lady.

Durante il primo mandato di Trump, Zampolli era stato nominato nel consiglio di amministrazione del Kennedy Center. Nella seconda amministrazione, il Presidente lo ha poi nominato rappresentante speciale degli Stati Uniti per le partnership globali. In questo ruolo, Zampolli avrebbe dovuto rappresentare gli Stati Uniti agli eventi culturali internazionali.

items.title: Guerra Ucraina - Russia, le news. Kiev: “Raid russi al confine con la Polonia, 370.000 senza luce”
items.summary: Costa a Zelensky: “Puoi contare su di noi”. Reuters: “L'ordine di rallentare Starlink all'Ucraina arrivato da dentro la Casa Bianca”
items.content:
Durante la notte, i raid dei droni russi hanno lasciato 370.000 persone senza elettricità nella regione ucraina della Volinia. Due persone sono rimaste ferite negli attacchi, che hanno colpito un'azienda con investimenti stranieri: lo ha dichiarato il governatore regionale su Telegram, come riporta Sky News Uk. La Volinia si trova nell'estremo ovest dell'Ucraina, al confine con la Polonia. In mattinata si sono udite esplosioni anche a Leopoli, scrive Rbc, causate dall'avvicinamento di un drone

Kallas: “Starlink ora è essenziale per Kiev, Ue non in grado di sostituirlo a breve”

Kiev: “Raid russi nella regione al confine con la Polonia, 370.000 senza luce”

Reuters: “L'ordine di rallentare Starlink all'Ucraina arrivato da dentro la Casa Bianca”

Trump, “Con attacchi a raffinerie Zelensky aumenta prezzi energia, uno scandalo”

Trump: “Non sono un fan di Zelensky, è più difficile di Putin”

Kallas: “Starlink ora è essenziale per Kiev, Ue non in grado di sostituirlo a breve”

"Starlink è davvero necessario per l'Ucraina e purtroppo, nel breve termine, l'Europa non è in grado di sostituire questa capacità". Lo ha dichiarato l'Alta rappresentante Ue Kaja Kallas, arrivando al Consiglio europeo. "Per questo oggi discutiamo anche della prontezza della difesa", ha spiegato, ricordando che "l'Agenzia europea per la difesa sta mappando tutte le capacità critiche e le lacune che dobbiamo colmare". "Ora si tratta di passare all'attuazione e dobbiamo farlo il prima possibile, perché abbiamo bisogno noi stessi di queste capacità", ha aggiunto. Le parole dell'Alta rappresentante Ue arrivano dopo le restrizioni di due giorni fa al servizio satellitare militare Starshield di SpaceX che hanno comportato interruzioni nelle comunicazioni dei droni ucraini e altre difficoltà militari per Kiev

Sugli asset russi congelati, "abbiamo concordato che tali beni non verranno restituiti finchè la Russia non avrà pagato le riparazioni all'Ucraina". Lo ha dichiarato l'Alta rappresentante dell'Ue per la Politica estera, Kaja Kallas, al suo arrivo al secondo giorno di vertice europeo. "L'Ucraina ha bisogno di queste risorse ora. Per questo stiamo lavorando a meccanismi di solidarietà che ripartiscano il rischio tra gli Stati membri, consentendoci così di fornire un aiuto concreto"

Un attacco sferrato dalle forze russe con droni e missili su Kharkiv ha causato tre morti e 13 feriti. Lo riferisce il capo dell'amministrazione militare della regione ucraina, Oleh Syniehubov. Un altro attacco russo a Sumy ha colpito un centro commerciale e causato due feriti

"Sono davvero grato per il sostegno immenso che riceviamo dal Consiglio europeo, dalla Commissione e dai leader europei. Veri leader, che ci sono rimasti accanto fin dall'inizio di questa guerra. E' un aspetto cruciale e noi contiamo su questo sostegno". Lo ha dichiarato il presidente ucraino, Volodymyr Zelensky, in un punto stampa con il presidente del Consiglio europeo Antonio Costa e la presidente della Commissione europea, Ursula von der Leyen, arrivando al secondo giorno di vertice europeo

Due persone sono rimaste uccise in seguito a attacchi di droni russi nel distretto di Shevchenko a Kharkiv.Lo afferma il sindaco di Kharkiv Igor Terekhov, ripreso dai media del paese. "Secondo le prime informazioni, due persone sono morte a seguito dell'attacco al distretto di Shevchenko. Nel distretto di Shevchenko si contano già 13 feriti", spiega il sindaco

L'obiettivo è aprire entro la fine dell'anno altri 2 cluster per l'adesione dell'Ucraina alla Ue. Lo ha detto la presidente della Commissione europea Ursula von der Leyen in un punto stampa congiunto con il presidente ucraino Vlodomyr Zelensky e il presidente del Consiglio europeo Antonio Costa. "L'obiettivo è entro la fine dell'anno di aprire gli ultimi due cluster per entrare davvero nel vivo dell'attuazione delle riforme necessarie per l'adesione" ha detto von der Leyen

Il presidente ucraino Vlodomyr Zelensky è arrivato all'Europa building per partecipare alla seconda giornata del Consiglio europeo. Ad accoglierlo il presidente del Consiglio europeo Antonio Costa

Kiev: “Raid russi nella regione al confine con la Polonia, 370.000 senza luce”

Durante la notte, i raid dei droni russi hanno lasciato 370.000 persone senza elettricità nella regione ucraina della Volinia. Due persone sono rimaste ferite negli attacchi, che hanno colpito un'azienda con investimenti stranieri: lo ha dichiarato il governatore regionale su Telegram, come riporta Sky News Uk. La Volinia si trova nell'estremo ovest dell'Ucraina, al confine con la Polonia. In mattinata si sono udite esplosioni anche a Leopoli, scrive Rbc, causate dall'avvicinamento di un drone

Le forze ucraine avrebbero colpito nella notte diversi obiettivi nelle regioni russe di Mosca, Rostov e Vladimir con un attacco su vasta scala condotto da droni. Secondo i canali ucraini di monitoraggio ExileNova+ e SuperNova+, il data center del colosso tecnologico russo Yandex nella regione di Vladimir, a circa 500 chilometri dal confine ucraino, è stato l'obiettivo dell'operazione notturna. I filmati ripresi dai residenti sul posto mostrano forti esplosioni e sistemi di difesa aerea in funzione intorno agli edifici residenziali

Reuters: “L'ordine di rallentare Starlink all'Ucraina arrivato da dentro la Casa Bianca”

L'ordine di limitare Starlink all'Ucraina è arivato da qualcuno all'interno della Casa Bianca. Lo riferiscono due funzionari americani alla Reuters sul suo sito, sottolineando che il Dipartimento della Difesa ha ricevuto la comunicazione che il servizio Starlink doveva essere rallentato

Trump, “Con attacchi a raffinerie Zelensky aumenta prezzi energia, uno scandalo”

Con gli attacchi alle raffinerie, Volodymyr Zelensky "aumenta i prezzi dell'energia, è uno scandalo. Ci sono molti altri obiettivi che si possono colpire". Lo ha detto Donald Trump in un'intervista a Newsmax rispondendo a chi gli chiedeva degli attacchi ucraini contro le raffinerie russe.

Trump: “Non sono un fan di Zelensky, è più difficile di Putin”

Zelensky "non è una persona facile con cui avere a che fare. Non sono un suo grande fan. Penso che sia più difficile avere a che fare con lui che con Vladimir Putin". Lo ha detto Donald Trump in un'intervista a Newsmax, ribadendo che servono elezioni in Ucraina. "Putin odia Zelensky e Zelensky odia Putin. Quando c'è questo tipo di odio è difficile risolvere le cose", ha aggiunto il presidente sottolineando che "se le elezioni" del 2020 non fossero state truccate, la guerra non sarebbe mai iniziata".

Nella città di Sepetivka (regione di Khmelnytskyi, nell'Ucraina occidentale) è scoppiato un incendio nei pressi di un deposito di petrolio a seguito di un attacco con i droni da parte delle forze armate russe. Lo ha comunicato su Telegram - come riporta il Kyiv Independent - il capo dell'amministrazione statale di Khmelnytskyi, Serhiy Tyurin: "A seguito dell'attacco, è scoppiato un incendio nell'area di un deposito di petrolio", si legge nel suo messaggio.

items.title: Manovra, 5 miliardi da banche e assicurazioni. Istituti sorpresi
items.summary: Misura non negoziata. La legge vale 23,5 miliardi, focus sugli aiuti alle famiglie
items.content:
La manovra parte da 23,5 miliardi di euro. Al centro la tutela del potere d'acquisto, soprattutto delle famiglie e dei più fragili, e gli investimenti delle imprese, sempre salvaguardando la sostenibilità dei conti pubblici. Proprio per questo le coperture sono essenziali: i ministeri faranno il loro con tagli di oltre un miliardo, i giochi daranno un contributo, ma la parte del leone è chiesta al settore finanziario. Il documento programmatico di bilancio, inviato nella notte dal Tesoro a Bruxelles, traccia lo scheletro della manovra.

Banche e assicurazioni saranno chiamate a contribuire con 5 miliardi nel 2027 e quasi 11 nel triennio. Una richiesta in qualche modo anticipata da membri del governo, in primis Matteo Salvini, ma che ora, messa nero su bianco, lascia il settore interdetto. Nessun commento ufficiale, ma da diverse fonti del mondo bancario trapela la contrarietà a un nuovo esborso dopo che lo scorso anno era stato raggiunto un accordo triennale per 10 miliardi di euro.

La notizia sarebbe arrivata senza alcuna negoziazione, senza preavviso e senza specificare come sarà diviso l'onere fra banche, assicurazioni e eventualmente altre società finanziarie. L'avrebbero spuntata, invece, le società energetiche, dopo il price cap volontario sui carburanti. L'incertezza è massima anche su quale potrebbe essere il tipo di intervento sugli istituti bancari, che potrebbe riguardare di nuovo le Dta (crediti scontabili in anni futuri) o altre misure. Forza Italia ha escluso un intervento sugli extraprofitti e chiede che la misura sia concordata. Soddisfazione trapela invece dalla Lega con Claudio Borghi che definisce il documento "un segnale positivo". Le maggiori voci della manovra saranno per le politiche per le famiglie e la spesa sociale, 5 miliardi. Nella tabella del Dpb, segue la difesa con 4,5 miliardi: un po' meno dello 0,3% del Pil previsto dalla flessibilità della Nec perchè lo 0,1% è già previsto nei tendenziali. Alla sanità vanno 2,4 miliardi. Per le infrastrutture (in cui confluirà parte della flessibilità per l'energia) sono stanziati 3,1 miliardi. Per le misure fiscali ci sono 2,16 miliardi, pochi per accontentare le richieste sul tavolo. Solo l'estensione dello scaglione Irpef al 33% fino a 60mila euro costa 2,7 miliardi, ma tra gli interventi più caldeggiati c'è anche la flat tax fino a 100mila euro e quella per i giovani, la detassazione delle tredicesime e degli aumenti contrattuali.

"La definizione puntuale degli interventi terrà conto degli esiti delle interlocuzioni in corso con le autorità europee", premette il testo. La presidente del Consiglio, Giorgia Meloni, è a Bruxelles al Consiglio europeo a far sentire le proprie ragioni. L'obiettivo è ottenere qualche margine in più per rimpolpare una manovra che, per ora, è la più magra degli ultimi quattro anni, lontana dal provvedimento elettorale in cui molti nella maggioranza avevano sperato fino a qualche tempo fa. Lo scenario internazionale ha del resto imposto la massima prudenza, tra tensioni geopolitiche, crisi energetica, inflazione e tensioni sui titoli di stato.

L'opposizione la vede però diversamente e interpreta il Documento programmatico di bilancio come "il conto del fallimento di Meloni", con le parole del presidente dei senatori dem, Francesco Boccia, che denuncia una crescita insufficiente, debito in crescita e salari reali al palo. Gli risponde il collega Giorgio Salvitti di Fratelli d'Italia: "prendi solo i dati che ti fanno comodo e descrivi l'apocalisse economica alle porte". Secondo il deputato di Avs Angelo Bonelli "per Meloni un carro armato vale più di cinque pronto soccorso" perché i fondi della manovra per la sanità sono circa 2,4 miliardi e quelli per la difesa 4,6 miliardi. Mentre per il leader di Noi Moderati, Maurizio Lupi "l'obiettivo della maggioranza è trasformare le risorse disponibili in risposte concrete per gli italiani".

items.title: What I self-host
items.summary: Article URL: https://viceconsole.fyi/blog/2026/10/10/what-i-self-host/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50109715 Points: 467 # Comments: 295
items.content:
I've always had a foot in the self-hosting world, long before it was called that. My freshman year of university, I ran a website from a Linux box underneath my bed. There was some downtime when my roommate got tired of the fan noise and turned it off. For several years I ran MythTV , then XBMC (later known as Kodi).

Recently, I lived for a few years in India, where streaming services are extremely inexpensive by western standards. We had Netflix, Disney Plus (Hotstar in India), and Spotify. After leaving India, I was unwilling to pay western prices for these services. But I had also become fed up with the engagement treadmill, particularly for my son. We wanted to limit his viewing choices to certain programming, but the constant "recommended for you" and "up next" caused conflict. While there are ways to limit content to specific titles, or disable auto-play, doing this for each service and keeping track of when client applications change and need to be reconfigured is too much work.

So, I "cut the cord" in a different sense, ditching streaming services for self-hosted Jellyfin . Over the course of the next year and a half, Jellyfin opened the door to self-hosting many other services, reducing my dependence on cloud service providers, and providing a welcome stability. No longer am I constantly confronted with unnecessary site redesigns, new features of questionable value, and a barrage of e-mails about terms-of-service updates, binding arbitration, data breaches, etc. I read the release notes of new versions of the software I host and decide if and when I want to upgrade.

With the exception of VPN servers that run on my router, I do not expose any services directly to the public internet. I don't care how convenient it would be, or how secure an application is. Especially with AI-assisted hacking, I simply don't think it's wise. My ISP also uses CGNAT for its IPv4 addresses, so my home network is not directly reachable from the public internet via IPv4. My VPN servers are only publicly routable on IPv6, a limitation that has some downsides but is workable for my use cases, and likely helps limit unfriendly attempted connections. The biggest downside is that my VPN will almost never function on a public Wifi network, since these rarely offer IPv6. When using my phone, I can disable Wi-Fi and connect over mobile data... if there is service.

I prefer running services natively when possible, but will containerize complex services or those with many dependencies. Love: a service that's a single Go binary. A service that only comes as a Docker compose file and wants to run MySQL, Redis, and three other containers? I'm already looking for an alternative. If the dependencies aren't overwhelming, native is better, faster, and more efficient. I can use the same management tools and commands across multiple services. There's no mental overhead of having to get into this container to run some command, finding out this container is missing curl, that one runs busybox so all the arguments are different, or dealing with a virtual network and host port mapping.

Related, I don't do Docker anymore. It's not really a principled position, but I grew tired of having to manage a completely separate service control system on my server. I'm already using systemd, and at this point Podman's integration with systemd is excellent.

Last year I bought a Beelink Mini PC, specifically an S12 Pro with an Intel N100 processor, 16 GB RAM, and a 512 GB internal SSD. It was before the rampocalypse, so I paid EUR 180. The same listing on Amazon is currently EUR 359. Ouch! Attached to the server is a 6 TB hard drive for media storage.

My comment on Hacker News about what I self-host prompted some questions about how all of this could run on 16 GB RAM. As I describe below, there are some choices I've made that reduce resource demand on my server, but ultimately it turns out you don't need much hardware to run a lot of stuff. Obviously I'm not running any local inference on this hardware, but for everything non-AI, it has just worked out of the box, or with some simple configuration tweaks.

Budgeting software with desktop clients and a web application, custom reports, and rules-based categorization. I only use this for budgeting and checking/savings/credit accounts. For tracking investment accounts, I use a cloud service. Some day I'll try to move away from the latter...

While Actual Budget supports automatic transaction import from various banks, I don't use this feature. Instead, after each month end, I download the prior month's transactions (OFX format preferred, CSV if no other option) and import them manually. This works for me because I primarily use Actual Budget for expense tracking, not... actual... budgeting.

Add, download and store audiobooks and podcasts on your server, listen to them on your phone. I haven't used the audiobook feature much, I set it up more for my kids, but it has very nice chapter handling. In the past for podcasts I used PlayerFM, then Pocket Casts, but now unless I'm out of the house without VPN connectivity, I use Audiobookshelf .

ARM automates ripping and transcoding DVDs (and Blu-rays, but I don't do those). Yes, it's 2026 and I still rip DVDs. Remember, we cut the cord, so not only is this a conduit for new-to-us content, but it's also a way for us to get bilingual content (English and French).

Web UI for Restic backup software. Backups are important! Especially for Immich (photos). Restic does a good job deduplicating and compressing backed up data, and Backrest makes it easy to manage the storage retention policies. Notifications in case of failure go to Gotify.

Beszel is a simple monitoring dashboard that collects basic stats from agents (in the old-fashioned sense of a small background service) to display CPU load, memory and disk usage, temperature, battery, etc. Helps me keep an eye on various other hosts I have around the house (several Rapsberry Pis and a Proxmox cluster that may be the subject of a future post).

Caddy is a web server and reverse proxy. Early on I didn't understand the value of a reverse proxy, and I thought I would be fine accessing my services with a local DNS name, or even IP address, and port number. But then I started adding more and more services, and some required HTTPS. So I got a domain name (not this one) and set up Caddy to automatically obtain LetsEncrypt SSL certificates, and now nearly all of my services are accessible on my LAN (or over VPN) with HTTPS and friendly subdomain names. Adding a new service is a quick edit to the Caddyfile.

Cockpit is a web-based admin console for the server. It uses normal system authentication methods. For me, it's mainly useful for spotting failed services when no notifications are set up for them.

Forgejo is a fork of Gitea, and deploys as a single binary. Github's uptime is the butt of a lot of jokes these days, but I also appreciate the speed of having my own git remote. Eventually I'll set up CI/CD and runners, if only to deploy this blog.

Web-based RSS reader . These days I basically visit two websites, though, so I've not been using it much. I do subscribe to the Github releases of some of the services I self-host so I can check out the features and bugfixes in new versions.

Network video recorder (NVR). I first started with Zoneminder because I'm of a certain age. But it became clear that Zoneminder is past its prime. Frigate has been fantastic. I run it with 8 IP cameras. It provides alerts for people and cars entering the driveway, integrates with Home Assistant to power various automations (e.g., when a person is detected in the backyard, turn on the camera floodlight). I may write a future post with some details about my IP camera adventures.

I run all of my cameras at lower resolutions than they support, primarily to avoid Wi-Fi network congestion. Most cameras also support an even lower-resolution RTSP substream, which is what Frigate uses for motion and object detection. Keeping the camera resolutions low avoids excessive CPU and memory from video processing, and excessive disk usage from recordings. They are good enough to identify faces, and privacy laws in my country prohibit filming public rights of way, so my cameras are not aimed at distant points.

Subsonic-compatible server written in Go. I purchased a perpetual Subsonic license a long time ago, but the original project is ancient and the modern alternatives are better. I run two separate instances of Gonic , one serves kid music, the other serves adult music.

Simple notification service written in Go. Many self-hosted services directly support Gotify notifications, or can send them via a custom HTTP POST. In conjunction with Uptime Kuma, I use Gotify to get notifications about any services or devices that are down, what my kids are watching on Jellyfin, when a new podcast episode is available in Audiobookshelf, etc.

Home Assistant probably deserves its own post. It's fantastic, and I cannot imagine trying to accomplish the same things within a proprietary ecosystem like Google Home, Amazon Alexa, or Apple Home. Things are better now that device manufacturers are standardizing on protocols like Matter, but the control and flexibility you get with Home Assistant is hard to beat. It has a steep learning curve, though, and I need to think about realistic ways to handle potential server failure without compromising the functionality of my home.
